## 7 Algorithms via 1-WL (Elementary Arguments)

In this section, we show that Constrained Shortest Path and Energy Game can be solved in near-linear time in the Isomorphic-Priors model using the 1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) algorithm. We start by formally defining both problems and stating the main algorithmic results for both problems. After that, we give an introduction to the 1-WL algorithm and prove our algorithmic results.

## 7.1 Constrained Shortest Path and Energy Game

**Definition 7.1** (Constrained Shortest Path (CSP))**.** An instance of Constrained Shortest Path is defined by a tuple \(G=(V,E,c,\ell,s,t,B)\), where:

• (_V,E_) is a finite directed graph.<tbc>

• \(c:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is a cost function assigning a non-negative cost to each edge.<tbc>

• \(\ell:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is a length (or delay) function assigning a non-negative length to each edge.<tbc>

• \(s,t\in V\) are the distinguished source and target vertices.<tbc>

• \(B\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) is the maximum allowable path cost constraint.

For a directed path _P_=(_e_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e<sub>r</sub>_) from _s_ to _t_, the total cost is \(c(P)=\sum_{i=1}^rc(e_i)\) and the total length is \(\ell(P)=\sum_{i=1}^r\ell(e_i)\). The objective is to find a feasible path _P_<sup>∗</sup> minimizing _c(P_<sup>∗</sup>) subject to \(\ell(P^*)\le B\). The optimal value is _OPT(G_)=_c(P_<sup>∗</sup>). If no path satisfies the length constraint, \(OPT(G)=\infty\).

Two problem instances \(G=(V,E,c,\ell,s,t,B)\) and \(G'=(V',E',c',\ell',s',t',B')\) of CSP are isomorphic if \(B=B'\) and their underlying graphs are isomorphic. Note that an isomorphism has to preserve vertex attributes and edge attributes (e.g., _s_ maps \(s'\), _t_ maps \(t'\), etc.).

Naturally, CSP with isomorphic priors is formalized as follows. In the preprocessing phase, we are given a database S={_G_<sub>1</sub>_,...,G<sub>k</sub>_} of _k_ prior instances. Each instance is given as a tuple \(G_i=(V_i,E_i,c_i,\ell_i,s_i,t_i,B_i)\), provided together with its optimal value _OPT(G<sub>i</sub>_). In the query phase, we receive a query graph \(G=(V,E,c,\ell,s,t,B)\).

**Theorem 7.2** (CSP in the Isomorphic-Priors Model)**.** _There is an algorithm that solves the_ CSP _problem with k prior instances each having at most n vertices and m edges in O(k(n+m_)log_n_) _preprocesses time and O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time. Additionally, if each prior G<sub>i</sub> is equipped with an optimal path, then the optimal path for the query graph can be found in O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time._

**Definition 7.3** (Energy Game)**.** An Energy Game instance is defined by a tuple _G_=(_V,E,V_<sub>1</sub>_,V_<sub>2</sub>_,w,v_<sub>0</sub>), where:

• (_V,E_) is a finite directed graph with no terminal states.<tbc>

• _V_<sub>1</sub>_,V_<sub>2</sub> is a partition of \(V(V_1\cup V_2=V\), \(V_1\cap V_2=\emptyset)\), where Player 1 controls _V_<sub>1</sub> and Player 2 controls _V_<sub>2</sub>.<tbc>

• \(w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}\) is a weight function assigning an integer energy change to each edge.<tbc>

• \(v_0\in V\) is the designated initial vertex.

A play \(\pi=v_0v_1v_2\dots\) is formed by moving a token: at step \(k\ge 0\), if \(v_k\in V_i\), Player _i_ chooses an outgoing edge \((v_k,v_{k+1})\in E\). Given an initial energy \(E_0\in\mathbb{N}\), the energy evolves via _E_<sub>_k_+1</sub>=_E<sub>k</sub>+w(v<sub>k</sub>,v_<sub>_k_+1</sub>). A strategy for Player 1 is winning from _v_<sub>0</sub> with initial energy _E_<sub>0</sub> if it ensures that \(E_k\ge 0\) for all \(k\ge 0\), regardless of the choices of Player 2. The objective is to find the minimum initial energy \(E_0^*\in\mathbb{N}\) for which Player 1 has a winning strategy from _v_<sub>0</sub>. The optimal value is \(OPT(G)=E_0^*\). If no finite initial energy allows Player 1 to win, we set \(OPT(G)=\infty\).

Two Energy Game instances _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic if their underlying graphs are isomorphic. Note that an isomorphism has to preserve vertex attributes and edge attributes. Therefore, Energy Game is closed under isomorphism.

**Theorem 7.4** (Energy Game in the Isomorphic-Priors Model)**.** _There is an algorithm that solves_ Energy Game _with k prior instances each having at most n vertices and m edges in O(k(n+m_)log_n_) _preprocesses time and O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time. Additionally, if each prior G<sub>i</sub>, that is a winning instance, is equipped with a memoryless winning strategy_ \(\sigma_i\) _for Player 1 from every starting vertex, then the algorithm can also compute a memoryless optimal winning strategy_ \(\sigma_H\) _with the same guarantees for H in O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _time._

## 7.2 Preliminaries: The Weisfeiler-Leman Algorithm

To solve constrained reachability and game dynamics, we model our problem instances as attributed directed graphs. Let \(G=(V,E,\alpha_V,\alpha_E)\) be a directed graph where \(\alpha_E:E\rightarrow\Sigma_E\) assigns an _attribute_ to each edge (e.g., costs, lengths, or weights), and \(\alpha_V:V\rightarrow\Sigma_V\) assigns an _attribute_ to each vertex (e.g. source, sink, or what player a vertex belongs to).

When initializing the _1-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (1-WL) algorithm_, the vertex attributes are directly translated into an initial vertex _coloring_, denoted by \(\chi_0^G:V\rightarrow\mathcal{C}\), such that \(\chi_0^G(u)=\chi_0^G(v)\) if and only if \(\alpha_V(u)=\alpha_V(v)\). The 1-WL algorithm then iteratively _refines_ these colors (e.g, by recolor some vertices of color _c_ with a new color _d_), ultimately returning a _stable color_ for every vertex _u_, denoted by \(\chi_\infty^G(u)\), which possesses the structural properties detailed in Lemma 7.6.

### The 1-WL Algorithm: A Primer.

The 1-WL algorithm can be intuitively understood as an iterative message-passing process. Initially, every vertex only knows its own starting color. In each round, every vertex "broadcasts" its current color to its neighbors. Simultaneously, it listens to the incoming messages, tallying up exactly how many neighbors of each color it has, grouped by the attributes and directions of the connecting edges. It then bundles its own current color with this exact tally to form a unique "signature". If two vertices that previously shared the same color generate different signatures (meaning their local neighborhoods differ), they are split into two different new colors. This process continues until no pair of vertices split into two different new colors. The final color is called the _stable color_.

Formally, let \(G=(V,E,\alpha_V,\alpha_E)\) be an attributed directed graph. For two colorings \(\chi,\chi':V\rightarrow\mathcal{C}\), we write \(\chi\unknown\chi'\) if \(\chi'(v)=\chi'(w)\) for all \(v,w\in V\) such that \(\chi(v)=\chi(w)\) (in other words, the partition into color classes of \(\chi\) refines the corresponding partition for \(\chi'\)). We write \(\chi\equiv\chi'\) if \(\chi\unknown\chi'\) and \(\chi'\unknown\chi\). The initial coloring computed by 1-WL is defined via \(\chi_0^G(v)=\alpha_V(v)\) for all \(v\in V(G)\). For \(i\ge 0\) the coloring is iteratively refined by setting

\(\chi_{i+1}^G(v):=\left(\chi_i^G(v),\left\{\left(\chi_i^G(u),\alpha_E(u,v)\right)|u\in N_{in}(v)\right\},\left\{\left(\chi_i^G(w),\alpha_E(v,w)\right)|w\in N_{out}(v)\right\}\right),\)

where {{_..._}} denotes a multiset. This refinement stabilizes when the partition of _V_ induced by the colors stops changing. More concretely, since \(\chi_{i+1}^G\unknown\chi_i^G\) for every \(i\ge 0\), there is some minimal \(i_\infty\ge 0\) such that \(\chi_{i_\infty}^G\equiv\chi_{i_\infty+1}^G\), and we set \(\chi_\infty^G:=\chi_{i_\infty+1}^G\). Note that we perform one extra iteration after stabilization, which is necessary for some technical reasons.

The 1-WL algorithm can be used as a simple heuristic to test isomorphisms of graphs. If some color appears a different number of times in the stable coloring of the two graphs, then they cannot be isomorphic (the converse is not true in general).

**Definition 7.5** (1-WL Equivalence)**.** Two (attributed) graphs _G_ and _H_ are _1-WL equivalent_ \((G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H)\) if \(\left\{\left(\chi_\infty^G(v)|v\in V(G)\right\}\right\}=\left\{\left(\chi_\infty^H(w)|w\in V(H)\right\}\).

### Properties of 1-WL.

Below are some basic facts about 1-WL.

**Lemma 7.6** (1-WL Properties; Folklore)**.** _For every two (attributed) graphs_ \(G=(V_G,E_G,\alpha_G^V,\alpha_G^E)\) _and_ \(H=(V_H,E_H,\alpha_H^V,\alpha_H^E)\) _such that_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\)_, the following holds:_

1. **_Refinement:_** _For every_ \(v\in V_G\) _and_ \(v'\in V_H\)_, if_ \(\chi_\infty^G(v)=\chi_\infty^H(v')\)_, then their initial colors match:_ \(\alpha_G^V(v)=\alpha_H^V(v')\).<tbc>

_2._ **_Neighborhood Preservation:_** _For every_ \(v\in V_G\) _and_ \(v'\in V_H\)_, if_ \(\chi_\infty^G(v)=\chi_\infty^H(v')\)_, then for every stable color C and edge attribute_ \(\ell\)_, there exists an incoming edge_ \((u,v)\in E_G\) _in G such that_ \(\alpha_G^E(u,v)=\ell\) _and_ \(\chi_\infty^G(u)=C\) _if and only if there exists an incoming edge_ \((u',v')\in E_H\) _in H such that_ \(\alpha_H^E(u',v')=\ell\) _and_ \(\chi_\infty^H(u')=C\)_. The analogous bi-conditional holds for outgoing edges._

_Remark_ 7.7. The 1-WL algorithm actually guarantees stronger properties than the above (see Lemma A.10). However, the properties above suffice to get results in this section.

_Proof Sketch of Lemma 7.6._ Let \(v\in V_G\) and \(v'\in V_H\) such that \(\chi_\infty^G(v)=\chi_\infty^H(v')\). Also let \(i_\infty\ge 0\) be minimal such that \(\chi_{i_\infty}^G\equiv\chi_{i_\infty+1}^G\). So \(\chi_\infty^G\equiv\chi_{i_\infty+1}^G\) and, since \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\) and \(\chi_\infty^G(v)=\chi_\infty^H(v')\), we also get that \(\chi_\infty^H\equiv\chi_{i_\infty+1}^H\). By definition, it holds for all \(i\ge 0\) that, if \(\chi_{i+1}^G(v)=\chi_{i+1}^H(v')\), then \(\chi_i^G(v)=\chi_i^H(v')\). So the first part follows by induction.

To prove Neighborhood Preservation, consider the coloring \(\chi^*:V(G)\unknown V(H)\rightarrow\mathcal{C}\) defined on the disjoint union of _G_ and _H_ via \(\chi^*(w):=\chi_\infty^G(w)\) for all \(w\in V(G)\), and \(\chi^*(w'):=\chi_\infty^H(w')\) for all \(w'\in V(H)\). Since \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\), it can be verified that the coloring \(\chi^*\) is stable for the disjoint union of _G_ and _H_, and in fact \(\chi_\infty^{G\unknown H}\equiv\chi^*\) (since all refinements being made on _G_ or _H_ also happen on \(G\unknown H\)). In particular, we get that \(\chi_\infty^{G\unknown H}(v)=\chi_\infty^{G\unknown H}(v')\). By definition, we conclude that

\(\left\{\left\{\left(\chi_\infty^{G\unknown H}(u),\alpha_G^E(u,v)\right)|u\in N_{in}(v)\right\}\right\}=\left\{\left\{\left(\chi_\infty^{G\unknown H}(u'),\alpha_H^E(u',v')\right)|u'\in N_{in}(v')\right\}\right\}.\)

In particular, a pair \((C,\ell)\) appears in the first set if and only if it appears in the second set.

By repeatedly applying Lemma 7.6 (Neighborhood Preservation), every sequence of valid steps in _G_ can be identically mirrored step-by-step in _H_. This sequential matching gives rise to the Walk Lifting property.

**Lemma 7.8** (Walk Lifting)**.** _Let_ \(G=(V_G,E_G,\alpha_G^V,\alpha_G^E)\) _and_ \(H=(V_H,E_H,\alpha_H^V,\alpha_H^E)\) _be (attributed) graphs such that_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\)_. Also let_ \(v_0\in V_G\) _and_ \(v'_0\in V_H\) _such that_ \(\chi_\infty^G(v_0)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_0)\)_. For every directed walk W_=(_v_<sub>0</sub>_,e_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e<sub>r</sub>,v<sub>r</sub>_) _in G, there exists a corresponding directed walk_ \(W'=(v'_0,e'_1,v'_1,\dots,e'_r,v'_r)\) _in H such that_ \(\chi_\infty^G(v_i)=\chi_\infty^H(v'_i)\) _for all_ \(0\le i\le r\)_, and_ \(\alpha_G^E(e_j)=\alpha_H^E(e'_j)\) _for all_ \(1\le j\le r\).

_Proof._ We proceed by induction on the length of the walk _r_.

In the case case _r_=0, the walk _W_ consists of a single vertex _v_<sub>0</sub>. We set \(W'\) to be the walk consisting only of \(v'_0\). By the lemma’s hypothesis, \(\chi_\infty^G(v_0)=\chi_\infty^H(v'_0)\), so the condition holds trivially.

So assume the claim holds for walks of length _k\<r_. Let _W<sub>k</sub>_=(_v_<sub>0</sub>_,...,e<sub>k</sub>,v<sub>k</sub>_) be the prefix of length _k_ in _G_, which by the inductive hypothesis lifts to a valid walk \(W'_k=(v'_0,\dots,e'_k,v'_k)\) in _H_ where \(\chi_\infty^G(v_k)=\chi_\infty^H(v'_k)\).

The next step in _W_ traverses the edge _e_<sub>_k_+1</sub>=(_v<sub>k</sub>,v_<sub>_k_+1</sub>) with some attribute \(\ell=\alpha_G^E(e_{k+1})\). Let \(C=\chi_\infty^G(v_{k+1})\) be the stable color of the destination vertex. By Lemma 7.6 (Neighborhood Preservation), since \(\chi_\infty^G(v_k)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_k)\), the existence of an outgoing edge from _v<sub>k</sub>_ to a vertex of color _C_ with attribute \(\ell\) guarantees the existence of an outgoing edge \(e'_{k+1}=(v'_k,v'_{k+1})\) in _H_ with attribute \(\alpha_H^E(e'_{k+1})=\ell\) such that \(\chi_\infty^H(v'_{k+1})=C\). Appending this edge \(e'_{k+1}\) and vertex \(v'_{k+1}\) to \(W'_k\) yields a valid walk of length _k_+1 satisfying all conditions.

### Runtime.

The straightforward mathematical definition of 1-WL constructs nested multisets as colors, leading to exponentially growing color representations (as strings) that are highly inefficient to compute and store. However, by replacing these unwieldy nested tuples with canonical integer identifiers at each iterative step, one obtains the near-linear runtimes required for our analysis \[CC82, PT87, BBG17\]. More precisely, we rely on the following result.

**Theorem 7.9** (\[BBG17\])**.** _There is an algorithm, that given an edge-labeled graph G, outputs a vertex-coloring_ \(\chi^G:V(G)\rightarrow[|V(G)|]\) _in time_

\(O((|V(G)|+|E(G)|)log|V(G)|)\)

_such that the following properties hold:_

1. _For every graph G it holds that_ \(\chi^G\equiv\chi_\infty^G\).<tbc>

_2._ _For every two graphs G,H such that_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}H\) _it holds that_ \((G,\chi^G)\equiv_{1\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}(H,\chi^H)\).<tbc>

_3._ _For every two isomorphic graphs G,H and every isomorphism_ \(\varphi:G\cong H\) _it holds that_ \(\chi^G(v)=\chi^H(\varphi(v))\) _for all_ \(v\in V(G)\).

Note that the output coloring can effectively be treated as the 1-WL coloring. One key difference is that, although \(\chi_\infty^G(v)\neq\chi_\infty^H(w)\), it may be that \(\chi^G(v)=\chi^H(w)\) since the exponentially growing color representations are compressed into a set of size _n_. However, this usually does not cause any problems.

The coloring from Theorem 7.9 can be used to obtain a _complete invariant_ for 1-WL equivalence (see, e.g., \[Ott17\]). For the Constrained Shortest Path and Energy Game (and other problems; see Appendix A), this gives a Invariant and Solution-Preserving Signature.

**Theorem 7.10.** _There is a deterministic algorithm that, given an attributed graph G, outputs a string_ \(\mathrm{WL}_1(G)\in\{0,1\}^*\) _in time O_((|_V(G_)|+|_E(G_)|)log|_V(G_)|)_, such that for every two input graphs G,H it holds that_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}H\) _if and only if_ WL<sub>1</sub>(_G_)=WL<sub>1</sub>(_H)._

_Proof Sketch._ On the input \(G=(V,E,\alpha_V,\alpha_E)\), we can compute the coloring \(\chi^G\) via Theorem 7.9. Now, we build the string \(\mathrm{WL}_1(G)\in\{0,1\}^*\) to encode the following information:

• For each color _a_ in the image \(\chi^G\), the size of \((\chi^G)^{-1}(a)\) and \(\alpha_V(v)\) for some (and thus for all) \(v\in(\chi^G)^{-1}(a)\) (in increasing order of colors \(a\in[|V(G)|]\)).<tbc>

• For each pair of colors \(a,a'\) in the image \(\chi^G\), and each edge attribute \(\ell\) in the image of \(\alpha_E\), the number of edges from \((\chi^G)^{-1}(a)\) to \((\chi^G)^{-1}(a')\) with edge attribute \(\ell\). If this number is zero, then we do not explicitly encode this information in the string.

Note that the resulting string has length at most _O_((|_V(G_)|+|_E(G_)|)log|_V(G_)|), and can be computed in the same time. It is easily seen that \(G\equiv_{1\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}H\) if and only if WL<sub>1</sub>(_G_)=WL<sub>1</sub>(_H_).

## 7.3 1-WL Equivalence Implies Equal Optimality

Now, let us return to Constrained Shortest Path and Energy Game. In order to prove Theorems 7.2 and 7.4 we argue that 1-WL equivalent instances achieve the same optimal value. As a result, it suffices to compute complete invariants for 1-WL for all priors, and store optimal solutions for them.<tbc>

**Theorem 7.11.** _Let_ \(G=(V,E,c:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},\ell:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},s,t,B)\text{\textit{and}}\)
\(G'=(V',E',c':E'\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},\ell':E'\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},s',t',B)\) _be two instances of the_ Constrained Shortest Path (CSP_) problem. If_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G'\)_, then they have the same optimal value for_ CSP. Before turning to the proof, let us recall how instances \(G=(V,E,c:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},\ell:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},s,t,B)\) of CSP are interpreted as attributed graphs. The attribute of each edge \(e\in E\) with length \(\ell(e)\) and cost _c(e_) is the vector \(\alpha_E(e)=(\ell(e),c(e))\). The vertex attributes designate the terminals: \(\alpha_V(v)=\mathsf{s}\) if _v_ is the source, \(\alpha_V(v)=\mathsf{t}\) if _v_ is the sink, and \(\alpha_V(v)=\perp\) otherwise. _Proof._ Let _OPT(G_) and \(OPT(G')\) denote the optimal values. By symmetry, it suffices to show \(OPT(G')\le OPT(G)\). If no feasible path exists in _G_, then \(OPT(G)=\infty\) and the inequality trivially holds. Assume a feasible optimal path exists, and let _P_=(_v_0_,e_1_,v_1_,...,er,vr_) be an optimal directed path in _G_ from _v_0=_s_ to _vr=t_ with total cost \(C\ge 0\) and length \(L\le B\). Recall that each edge _ej_ carries the attribute \(\alpha_E(e_j)=(c(e_j),\ell(e_j))\). Because \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G'\) and \(\alpha_V\) isolates the distinguished vertices into singleton color classes, we obtain that \(\chi_\infty^G(s)\) and \(\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(s')\). By Lemma 7.8 (Walk Lifting), there exists a directed walk \(W'=(v'_0,e'_1,v'_1,\dots,e'_r,v'_r)\) in \(G'\) starting at \(s'\) with the exact same sequence of edge attributes \((c,\ell)\) and stable vertex colors. In particular, \(\chi_\infty^G(t)=\chi_\infty^G(v_r)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_r)\). Since _t_ and \(t'\) are distinguished via \(\alpha_V\) and \(\alpha'_V\), we obtain that \(v'_r=t'\) by Lemma 7.6. The total cost and length of walk \(W'\) are identical to _P_, meaning \(W'\) is a feasible solution in \(G'\) with cost _C_. If \(W'\) contains cycles, they can be removed to form a simple directed path \(P'\). Given that the edge lengths and costs are non-negative, removing cycles cannot increase the total cost or violate the length constraint. Thus, \(OPT(G')\le C=OPT(G)\). **Theorem 7.12.** _Let G_=(_V,E,V_1_,V_2_,w,v_0) _and_ \(G'=(V',E',V'_1,V'_2,w',v'_0)\) _be two_ Energy Game _instances. If_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G'\)_, then Player 1 has a winning strategy in G from v_0 _with initial energy E_0 _if and only if Player 1 has a winning strategy in_ \(G'\) _from_ \(v'_0\) _with initial energy E_0. Again, let us first recall how instances _G_=(_V,E,V_1_,V_2_,w,v_0) are interpreted as attributed graphs. The attribute of each edge \(e\in E\) is \(\alpha_E(e)=w(e)\). The vertex attributes indicate the partition according to players and the initial vertex: \(\alpha_V(v)=(i,\mathsf{s})\) if _v_ is the initial vertex, and \(\alpha_V(v)=(i,\perp)\) otherwise, where in both cases \(i\in\{1,2\}\) is the unique index such that \(v\in V_i\). _Proof._ By symmetry, it suffices to show that if Player 1 has a winning strategy \(\sigma\) in _G_ starting at _v_0 with energy _E_0, they also have a winning strategy \(\sigma'\) in \(G'\) starting at \(v'_0\) with energy _E_0. We define \(\sigma'\) dynamically by maintaining a simulated "shadow play" in _G_. Let the current finite prefix of the play in \(G'\) be \(\pi'=(v'_0,\dots,v'_k)\) and the maintained shadow play in _G_ be \(\pi=(v_0,\dots,v_k)\). We enforce the invariant that \(\chi_\infty^G(v_i)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_i)\) and \(w(v_{i-1},v_i)=w'(v'_{i-1},v'_i)\) for all \(i\le k\). 1. **Base Case:** For _k_=0, the play begins at \(v'_0\). We set the shadow play to _v_0. Since \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G'\), we conclude that \(\chi_\infty(v'_0)=\chi_\infty(v_0)\) using Lemma 7.6 (Refinement). 2. **Player 1’s Turn:** Suppose the current play is at \(v'_k\in V'_1\). Because colors strictly preserve initial partitions (by Lemma 7.6, Refinement), the shadow vertex _vk_ satisfies \(v_k\in V_1\). In _G_, strategy \(\sigma\) dictates an outgoing edge (_vk,v__k_+1) with weight _W_. By Lemma 7.6 (Neighborhood Preservation), since \(\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_k)=\chi_\infty^G(v_k)\), there exists an outgoing edge in \(G'\) to some vertex \(v'_{k+1}\) such that \(\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_{k+1})=\chi_\infty^G(v_{k+1})\) and \(w'(v'_k,v'_{k+1})=W\). Player 1’s strategy \(\sigma'\) chooses this edge, and we append _v__k_+1 to the shadow play.

3. **Player 2’s Turn:** Suppose the current play is at \(v'_k\in V'_2\), meaning the shadow vertex _v<sub>k</sub>_ satisfies \(v_k\in V_2\). Player 2 chooses an arbitrary edge \((v'_k,v'_{k+1})\) with weight _W_. By Lemma 7.6 (Neighborhood Preservation), since \(\chi_\infty^G(v_k)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_k)\), there exists an outgoing edge from _v<sub>k</sub>_ to some vertex _v_<sub>_k_+1</sub> in _G_ such that \(\chi_\infty^G(v_{k+1})=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_{k+1})\) and _w(v<sub>k</sub>,v_<sub>_k_+1</sub>)=_W_. We append this _v_<sub>_k_+1</sub> to the shadow play.

Through this induction, every infinite play \(\pi'\) in \(G'\) conforming to \(\sigma'\) maps to a valid shadow play \(\pi\) in _G_ conforming to \(\sigma\). Crucially, the sequence of edge weights traversed in \(\pi'\) is identical to that in \(\pi\). Because \(\sigma\) is winning in _G_, the energy level along \(\pi\) satisfies \(E_k\ge 0\) for all \(k\ge 0\). Since the step-by-step weights match exactly, the energy level in \(G'\) also satisfies \(E'_k=E_k\ge 0\) for all \(k\ge 0\). Thus, \(\sigma'\) is a winning strategy for Player 1 in \(G'\).

## 7.4 Proof of Theorems 7.2 and 7.4

_Proof of Theorem 7.2._ We describe the different phases of the algorithm.

**Preprocessing:** For each graph \(G_i\in\mathcal{S}\), we run the 1-WL algorithm (Theorem 7.9) and compute its complete invariant for 1-WL equivalence (Theorem 7.10). Both subroutines run in time _O_((_n+m_)log_n_) time. We insert each string \(\mathrm{WL}_1(G_i)\in\{0,1\}^*\) into a binary search tree, where the _i_-th letter determines whether we take the left/right subtree on the _i_-th level. This takes time proportional to the length of the string WL<sub>1</sub>(_G<sub>i</sub>_), i.e., it can be done in time _O_((_n+m_)log_n_). For the corresponding node where the key WL<sub>1</sub>(_G<sub>i</sub>_) is saved, we save the _OPT<sub>i</sub>_ as well as an optimal solution path (if provided) and the stable coloring \(\chi^{G_i}\).

Note that, if two graphs \(G_i,G_j\in\mathcal{S}\) yield the same invariant, they are 1-WL equivalent (Theorem 7.10). In particular, by Theorem 7.11, this implies _OPT<sub>i</sub>=OPT<sub>j</sub>_, and no conflicting values can be assigned to a single node of the search tree. Overall, processing all _k_ graphs takes _O(k(n+m_)log_n_) time.

**Query:** Given the query graph _H_, we run the 1-WL algorithm (Theorem 7.9) and compute its complete invariant for 1-WL equivalence (Theorem 7.10) in _O_((_n+m_)log_n_) time. Looking up the computed invariant in the binary search tree takes _O_((_n+m_)log_n_) time, allowing us to return _OPT(H_)=_OPT<sub>i</sub>_ (which is correct by Theorem 7.11). If the string WL<sub>1</sub>(_H_) is not contained in the search tree, then we can correctly claim that _H_ is not isomorphic to any graph in S because graphs that are not 1-WL equivalent are not isomorphic. The total query time is _O_((_n+m_)log_n_).

**Reconstruction:** If optimal paths are stored, the lookup yields the optimal path _P<sub>i</sub>_=(_v_<sub>0</sub>_,e_<sub>1</sub>_,v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,e<sub>r</sub>,v<sub>r</sub>_) from the equivalent graph _G<sub>i</sub>_. Because \(H\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G_i\), analogous to the proof of Theorem 7.11, we can inductively construct a correspondind walk in _H_: if we are currently at \(u'\in V(H)\) corresponding to \(v_j\in P_i\), we scan the outgoing edges of \(u'\) to find an edge \(e'\) with the same attributes as _e_<sub>_j_+1</sub> that leads to a vertex \(v'\) with the same 1-WL stable color as _v_<sub>_j_+1</sub>. The existence of such an edge is guaranteed by Lemma 7.6 (Neighborhood Preservation). Scanning for the next edge takes time proportional to the out-degree of the current vertex. Over the entire path, this takes at most _O(n+m_) time. This procedure yields a valid walk \(W'\) in _H_ with identical cost and length to _P<sub>i</sub>_. Finally, we remove cycles from \(W'\) in _O(n_) time to produce a simple optimal path _P<sub>H</sub>_. The total query time for the path remains _O_((_n+m_)log_n_).

We now turn from the proof of CSP to the proof of Theorem 7.4. The shadow play construction in the proof of Theorem 7.12 may use memory, even when the original strategy is memoryless. To reconstruct memoryless strategies, we therefore use color-consistent strategies, defined as follows.

**Definition 7.13** (Color-Consistent Strategy)**.** Let _G_=(_V,E,V_<sub>1</sub>_,V_<sub>2</sub>_,w,v_<sub>0</sub>) be an Energy Game instance with stable 1-WL coloring \(\chi_\infty^G\). A memoryless strategy \(\sigma\) of Player 1 is _color-consistent_ if,<tbc>

for all \(u,v\in V_1\) with \(\chi_\infty^G(u)=\chi_\infty^G(v)\),

\(\chi_\infty^G(\sigma(u))=\chi_\infty^G(\sigma(v))\text{and}w(u,\sigma(u))=w(v,\sigma(v)).\)

The following lemma, whose proof is deferred to Appendix A.1, shows that a memoryless strategy optimal from every vertex can be made color-consistent in linear time, given the stable 1-WL coloring.

**Lemma 7.14.** _Let G_=(_V,E,V_<sub>1</sub>_,V_<sub>2</sub>_,w,v_<sub>0</sub>) _be an_ Energy Game _instance with n vertices and m edges. Suppose we are given its stable 1-WL coloring_ \(\chi_\infty^G\) _and a memoryless strategy_ \(\sigma\) _of Player 1 that wins from every vertex with the minimum possible initial energy. Then a color-consistent memoryless strategy_ \(\widehat{\sigma}\) _with the same optimality property can be computed in O(n+m_) _time._

_Proof of Theorem 7.4._ We describe the different phases of the algorithm.

**Preprocessing:** For each graph \(G_i\in\mathcal{S}\), we run the 1-WL algorithm (Theorem 7.9) and compute its complete invariant for 1-WL equivalence (Theorem 7.10). Both subroutines run in time _O_((_n+m_)log_n_) time. We insert each string \(\mathrm{WL}_1(G_i)\in\{0,1\}^*\) into a binary search tree, where the _i_-th letter determines whether we take the left/right subtree on the _i_-th level. This takes time proportional to the length of the string WL<sub>1</sub>(_G<sub>i</sub>_), i.e., it can be done in time _O_((_n+m_)log_n_). For the corresponding node where the key WL<sub>1</sub>(_G<sub>i</sub>_) is saved, we save _WIN<sub>i</sub>=OPT(G<sub>i</sub>_) and the stable coloring \(\chi^{G_i}\). If an optimal memoryless strategy \(\sigma_i\) is provided, we apply Lemma 7.14 to compute and store a color-consistent optimal memoryless strategy \(\widehat{\sigma}_i\). This additional step takes _O(m+n_) time.

Note that, if two graphs \(G_i,G_j\in\mathcal{S}\) yield the same invariant, they are 1-WL equivalent (Theorem 7.10). In particular, by Theorem 7.12, this guarantees _WIN<sub>i</sub>=WIN<sub>j</sub>_, so no conflicting values can be assigned to a single node of the search tree. Overall, processing all _k_ graphs takes _O(k(n+m_)log_n_) time.

**Query:** Given the query graph _H_, we run the 1-WL algorithm (Theorem 7.9) and compute its complete invariant for 1-WL equivalence (Theorem 7.10) in _O_((_n+m_)log_n_) time. Looking up the computed invariant in the binary search tree takes _O_((_n+m_)log_n_) time, allowing us to return _OPT(H_)=_WIN<sub>i</sub>_ (which is correct by Theorem 7.12). If the string WL<sub>1</sub>(_H_) is not contained in the search tree, then we can correctly claim that _H_ is not isomorphic to any graph in S because graphs that are not 1-WL equivalent are not isomorphic. The total query time is _O_((_n+m_)log_n_).

**Reconstruction:** Suppose \(OPT(G_i)<\infty\) and a color-consistent optimal memoryless strategy \(\widehat{\sigma}_i\) is stored. For each Player 1 color class _C_ in _G<sub>i</sub>_, choose a representative _u<sub>C</sub>_ and set \(v_C=\widehat{\sigma}_i(u_C)\). For every Player 1 vertex \(u'\in V_H\) with \(\chi_\infty^H(u')=C\), choose a successor \(v'\) satisfying

\(w_H(u',v')=w_i(u_C,v_C)\text{and}\chi_\infty^H(v')=\chi_\infty^{G_i}(v_C),\)

and define \(\sigma_H(u')=v'\). Such a successor exists by Lemma 7.6 (Neighborhood Preservation). Selecting representatives and scanning the outgoing edges of Player 1 vertices takes _O(n+m_) time, using the color identifiers computed by Theorem 7.9.

To prove correctness, consider any walk \(u'_0u'_1\dots\) consistent with \(\sigma_H\), and choose \(u_0\in V(G_i)\) with \(\chi_\infty^{G_i}(u_0)=\chi_\infty^H(u'_0)\). As in the proof of Theorem 7.12, we construct a shadow walk _u_<sub>0</sub>_u_<sub>1</sub>_..._ in _G<sub>i</sub>_ with matching vertex colors and edge weights. At Player 1 vertices, color consistency ensures that \(\widehat{\sigma}_i(u_k)\) has the same successor color and edge weight as the move chosen by \(\sigma_H\) at \(u'_k\). At Player 2 vertices, Neighborhood Preservation supplies a matching edge. Hence the shadow walk is consistent with \(\widehat{\sigma}_i\).

The shadow-play argument in both directions shows that equally colored vertices have the same minimum initial energy. Since \(\widehat{\sigma}_i\) is optimal from every starting vertex and the two walks have identical edge weights, \(\sigma_H\) is optimal from every starting vertex as well. In particular, it wins from the designated initial vertex with energy _OPT(H_)=_OPT(G<sub>i</sub>_). The total query time remains _O_((_n+m_)log_n_).

## 8 More on Weisfeiler-Leman (Advanced Arguments)

The two algorithms from Section 7 highlight a general approach for obtaining algorithms in the Isomorphic-Priors model: if optimal solution values are preserved under WL equivalence (see, e.g., Theorems 7.11 and 7.12), then we obtain efficient algorithms in our model. This strategy is not limited to 1-WL, but also holds for higher-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman. More precisely, for each \(\ell\ge 1\), the \(\ell\)-dimensional Weisfeiler-Leman (\(\ell\)-WL) algorithm is a heuristic for graph isomorphism testing that accumulates information by coloring \(\ell\)-tuples of vertices. For increasing \(\ell\ge 1\), the algorithm becomes more expressive, but it also becomes computationally more expensive.

In this section, we present a systematic way to use the \(\ell\)-WL algorithm within the Isomorphic- Priors model. After describing the algorithm in Section 8.1, we begin by showing in Section 8.2 that every problem \(\Pi\) that is invariant under \(\ell\)-WL is polynomial time solvable inside the Isomorphic- Priors model (see Theorems 8.3 and 8.4). We then develop a technique that helps us prove when a problem is in fact \(\ell\)-WL invariant.

In Section 8.3 and Section 8.4, we apply this technique to the CSP and CST problems and show that they are 1-WL invariant and 2-WL invariant, respectively. As a result, we obtain fast algorithms for both problems in the Isomorphic-Priors model. Furthermore, additional examples are discussed in Appendix A. However, the Weisfeiler-Leman algorithm has its limits. In Section 8.5, we present an example of a problem that lies in P (and can therefore be efficiently solved in the Isomorphic-Priors model) but that is not \(\ell\)-WL invariant for any constant \(\ell\). This means that Weisfeiler-Leman cannot be used to obtain a fast algorithm for this problem in the Isomorphic-Priors model.

### 8.1 The Weisfeiler-Leman Algorithm

We start with a description of the \(\ell\)-WL algorithm (see, e.g., \[GN21, Kie20b, Kie20a\]). Fix some \(\ell\ge 2\) and let \(G=(V,E,\alpha_V,\alpha_E)\) be an attributed graph. For two colorings \(\chi,\chi':V^\ell\rightarrow\mathcal{C}\), we say \(\chi\) _refines_ \(\chi'\), denoted \(\chi\unknown\chi'\), if \(\chi(\bar{v})=\chi(\bar{w})\) implies \(\chi'(\bar{v})=\chi'(\bar{w})\) for all \(\bar{v},\bar{w}\in V^\ell\). The colorings \(\chi\) and \(\chi'\) are _equivalent_, denoted \(\chi\equiv\chi'\), if \(\chi\unknown\chi'\) and \(\chi'\unknown\chi\).

We define the initial coloring \(\chi_0^{G,\ell}:V^\ell\rightarrow\mathcal{C}\) computed by \(\ell\)-WL as the coloring where each tuple is colored with the isomorphism type of its underlying ordered subgraph. More precisely, for a second attributed graph \(G'=(V',E',\alpha'_V,\alpha'_E)\), and vertices \(v_1,\dots,v_\ell\in V\) and \(v'_1,\dots,v'_\ell\in V'\) we have \(\chi_0^{G,\ell}(v_1,\dots,v_\ell)=\chi_0^{G^\prime,\ell}(v'_1,\dots,v'_\ell)\) if and only if, for all \(i,j\in[\ell]\), we have

• _v<sub>i</sub>=v<sub>j</sub>_ if and only if \(v'_i=v'_j\),<tbc>

• \(\alpha_V(v_i)=\alpha'_V(v'_i)\),<tbc>

• \((v_i,v_j)\in E\) if and only if \((v'_i,v'_j)\in E'\), and<tbc>

• if \((v_i,v_j)\in E\), then \(\alpha_E(v_i,v_j)=\alpha'_E(v'_i,v'_j)\).

<tbc>We then recursively define the coloring \(\chi_i^{G,\ell}\) obtained after _i_ rounds of the algorithm. For \(\bar{v}=(v_1,\dots,v_k)\in V^\ell\), set<tbc>

\(\chi_{i+1}^{G,\ell}(\bar{v}):=\big(\chi_i^{G,\ell}(\bar{v}),\mathcal{M}_i(\bar{v})\big),\)

<tbc>where

\(\mathcal{M}_i(\bar{v}):=\big\{\big(\chi_i^{G,\ell}(\bar{v}[w/1]),\dots,\chi_i^{G,\ell}(\bar{v}[w/\ell])\big)\big|w\in V\big\}\)

and \(\bar{v}[w/i]:=(v_1,\dots,v_{i-1},w,v_{i+1},\dots,v_\ell)\) is the tuple obtained from substituting the _i_-th entry of \(\bar{v}\) with _w_. By definition, \(\chi_{i+1}^{G,\ell}\unknown\chi_i^{G,\ell}\) holds for all \(i\ge 0\). So there is a minimal \(i_\infty\ge 0\) such that \(\chi_{i_\infty}^{G,\ell}\equiv\chi_{i_\infty+1}^{G,\ell}\), and we set \(\chi_\infty^{G,\ell}:=\chi_{i_\infty+1}^{G,\ell}\).

**Definition 8.1** (\(\ell\)-WL Equivalence)**.** Two (attributed) graphs _G_ and _H_ are \(\ell\)_-WL equivalent_ \((G\equiv_{\ell\text{-}\text{WL}}H)\) if \(\left\{\left\{\chi_\infty^{G,\ell}(\bar{v})|\bar{v}\in(V(G))^\ell\right\}=\left\{\left\{\chi_\infty^{H,\ell}(\bar{w})|\bar{w}\in(V(H))^\ell\right\}\right\}\).

Observe that isomorphic (attributed) graphs _G,H_ are always \(\ell\)-WL equivalent.

Given an (attributed) graph _G_, the coloring \(\chi_\infty^{G,\ell}\) can be computed in time \(O(n^{\ell+1}logn)\) \[IL90\] (more precisely, similar to Theorem 7.9, we compute a coloring equivalent to \(\chi_\infty^{G,\ell}\)). Moreover, similar to Theorem 7.10, we can compute a complete invariant for \(\ell\)-WL equivalence (see, e.g., \[Ott17\]). In turn, this can be used as an Invariant and Solution-Preserving Signature for problems such as Constrained Spanning Tree (see Section 8.4).

**Theorem 8.2.** _Let_ \(\ell\ge 2\)_. There is a deterministic algorithm that, given an attributed graph G, outputs a string_ \(\text{WL}_\ell(G)\in\{0,1\}^*\) _in time_ \(O(|V(G)|^{\ell+1}log|V(G)|)\)_, such that for every two input graphs G,H it holds that_ \(G\equiv_{\ell\text{-}\text{WL}}H\) _if and only if_ \(\text{WL}_\ell(G)=\text{WL}_\ell(H)\).

## 8.2 \(\ell\)-WL Invariant Functions are in the Isomorphic-Priors Model

A function _f_ on (attributed) graphs is called \(\ell\)_-WL invariant_ if _f(G_)=_f(H_) for all (attributed) graphs _G,H_ with \(G\equiv_{\ell\text{-}\text{WL}}H\).<sup>25</sup> We say that an optimization problem \(\Pi\) is \(\ell\)_-WL invariant_ if \(OPT_\Pi\) is \(\ell\)-WL invariant (where \(OPT_\Pi\) denotes the function that maps an (attributed) input graph to the value of an optimum solution). For such problems, we obtain polynomial-time algorithm in the Isomorphic-Priors model using similar arguments as in Section 7.

**Theorem 8.3.** _Let_ \(\ell\ge 2\) _and let_ \(\Pi\) _be an optimization problem that is_ \(\ell\)_-WL invariant._

_Then there is an algorithm that solves_ \(\Pi\) _with k prior instances each of size at most n in_ \(O(kn^{\ell+1}logn)\) _preprocessing time and_ \(O(n^{\ell+1}logn)\) _query time._

_Proof._ Write S:={_G<sub>i</sub>_}<sub>_i_=1_...k_</sub> for the prior instances. We describe the different phases of the algorithm.

**Preprocessing:** For each graph \(G_i\in\mathcal{S}\), we compute a complete invariant \(\text{WL}_\ell(G)\in\{0,1\}^*\) for _G<sub>i</sub>_ using Theorem 8.2 in time \(O(n^{\ell+1}logn)\) time. We insert each string \(\text{WL}_\ell(G_i)\in\{0,1\}^*\) into a binary search tree, where the _i_-th letter determines whether we take the left/right subtree on the _i_-th level. This takes time proportional to the length of the string \(\text{WL}_\ell(G_i)\), i.e., it can be done in time \(O(n^{\ell+1}logn)\). For the corresponding node where the key \(\text{WL}_\ell(G_i)\) is saved, we save \(OPT_\Pi(G_i)\).

Note that, if two graphs \(G_i,G_j\in\mathcal{S}\) have the same complete invariant, they are \(\ell\)-WL equivalent (Theorem 8.2). In particular, since \(\Pi\) is \(\ell\)-WL invariant, we get that \(OPT_\Pi(G_i)=OPT_\Pi(G_j)\), and no conflicting values can be assigned to a single node of the search tree. Overall, processing all _k_ graphs takes \(O(kn^{\ell+1}logn)\) time.

**Query:** Given the query graph _H_, we compute a complete invariant \(\text{WL}_\ell(H)\in\{0,1\}^*\) for _G<sub>i</sub>_ using Theorem 8.2 in time \(O(n^{\ell+1}logn)\) time. Looking up the computed invariant in the binary search tree takes \(O(n^{\ell+1}logn)\) time, allowing us to return \(OPT_\Pi(H)=OPT_\Pi(G_i)\) (which is correct since \(\Pi\) is \(\ell\)-WL invariant). If the string \(\text{WL}_\ell(H)\) is not contained in the search tree, then we can correctly claim that _H_ is not isomorphic to any graph in S because graphs that are not \(\ell\)-WL equivalent are not isomorphic. The total query time is \(O(n^{\ell+1}logn)\).

For 1-WL invariant optimization problems, we obtain the following variant which is proved analogously using Theorem 7.10.

**Theorem 8.4.** _Let_ \(\Pi\) _be an optimization problem that is 1-WL invariant. Then there is an algorithm that solves_ \(\Pi\) _with k prior instances each of size at most n in O(k(n+m_)log_n_) _preprocessing time and O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time._

<sup>25</sup>In the literature (see, e.g., \[GGR24\]), the minimal \(\ell\ge 1\) (if it exists) such that _f_ is \(\ell\)-WL invariant is also called the _WL dimension_ of _f_.

We note that, in Theorems 7.2 and 7.4, we can also reconstruct an optimal solution of a query graphs if we are given optimal solutions for all priors. While it does not seem possible to obtain such a statement in the general setting of Theorems 8.3 and 8.4, we note that all our arguments for specific problems do imply that optimal solutions can indeed be reconstructed (see Appendix A for further examples).

In the following, we use an alternative way to characterize when an optimization problem is \(\ell\)-WL invariant. We limit ourself to minimization problems. However, our approach can easily be extended to maximization problems. Remember that G is the set of valid attributed input graphs.

**Definition 8.5.** Let \(\Pi\) be an minimization problem. We call a triple \((W,\text{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},\text{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) a _witness function of_ \(OPT_\Pi\) if:

• For all _G_ and \(X\in W\): if check(_G,X)\>_0 then \(OPT_\Pi(G)\le\text{cost}(X)\).<tbc>

• If \(OPT_\Pi(G)<\infty\) then there is a \(X\in W\) with \(OPT_\Pi(G)=\text{cost}(X)\) and check(_G,X)\>_0.

The intuition behind \((W,\text{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},\text{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) is that it characterizes the witnesses of the minimization problem \(\Pi\). The function "check" checks for an element _X_ if there exist a feasible solution (which is the case if check(_G,X)\>_0) with cost at most cost(_X_). Further, if _G_ has a feasible solution (i.e. \(OPT_\Pi(G)<\infty\)) then there is a _witness_ \(X\in G\) that attains the optimal value (i.e. \(OPT_\Pi(G)=\text{cost}(X)\) and check(_G,X)\>_0).

In the following, we show that we can a witness function to show that \(OPT_\Pi\) is \(\ell\)-WL. To this end, we show that the witness function itself is \(\ell\)-WL invariant.

**Definition 8.6.** Let \(\text{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) be a function. We say that check is \(\ell\)_-WL invariant on_ G if: for all graphs \(G,H\in\mathcal{G}\) with \(G\equiv_{\ell\text{-WL}}H\) and all \(X\in W\) we obtain that check(_G,X)\>_0 if and only if check(_H,X)\>_0.

**Lemma 8.7.** _Let_ \(\Pi\) _be an minimization problem and_ \((W,\text{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0},\text{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) _be a witness function of_ \(OPT_\Pi\)_. If_ check _is_ \(\ell\)_-WL invariant on_ G _then_ \(\Pi\) _is_ \(\ell\)_-WL invariant._

_Proof._ Let \(G,H\in\mathcal{G}\) be two graphs with \(G\equiv_{\ell\text{-WL}}H\). Without loss of generality, we assume \(OPT_\Pi(G)\le OPT_\Pi(H)\) (otherwise we change to role of _G_ and _H_). We have to show that \(OPT_\Pi(H)\le OPT_\Pi(G)\). If \(OPT_\Pi(G)=\infty\) then we are already done. Otherwise, \(OPT_\Pi(G)<\infty\). Thus, there exist a \(X\in W\) with \(OPT_\Pi(G)=\text{cost}(X)\) and check(_G,X)\>_0. Now, since check is \(\ell\)-WL invariant, we obtain that check(_H,X)\>_0. Hence, \(OPT_\Pi(H)\le\text{cost}(X)=OPT_\Pi(G)\).

## 8.3 CSP is 1-WL Invariant

We first demonstrate the above approach on the Constrained Shortest Path (CSP) problem and present an alternative proof for Theorem 7.2 using a characterization of 1-WL via homomorphism counts \[Dvo10, DGR18\]. Write _OPT_ for the optimal value function of CSP and G for the set of valid input graphs of CSP. We show that _OPT_ is 1-WL invariant for all values.<sup>26</sup> This together with Theorem 8.4 immediately yields that CSP is in the Isomorphic-Priors model.

**Theorem 8.8.** _The Problem_ CSP _is 1-WL invariant._

To prove Theorem 8.8 we define a witness for _OPT_ and show that this witness is 1-WL invariant. To this end, we start by defining graph homomorphisms.

<sup>26</sup>There is the small technical detail that an input graph _G_ has a length constraint _B_ that is part of the input. Consistent with previous sections, we say that two input graphs _G_ and _H_ are 1-WL equivalent if _G_ and _H_ have the same length constraint _B_ and \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\) for the underlying attributed graphs.

**Definition 8.9** (Homomorphism of attributed Graphs)**.** Let

\(G=(V_G,E_G,\alpha_G^V,\alpha_G^E)\text{and}H=(V_H,E_H,\alpha_H^V,\alpha_H^E)\)

be two graphs, where _V<sub>G</sub>,V<sub>H</sub>_ are vertex sets, _E<sub>G</sub>,E<sub>H</sub>_ are edge sets, and \(\alpha^V,\alpha^E\) assign attributes from alphabets \(\Sigma_V,\Sigma_E\) to the vertices and edges, respectively.

We say that a function \(f:V_H\rightarrow V_G\) is a _homomorphism_ from _H_ to _G_ if:

1. **Adjacency is preserved:** For all \((u,v)\in E_H\) it is true that \((\varphi(u),\varphi(v))\in E_G\).<tbc>

2. **Vertex attributes are preserved:** For all \(u\in H\) it is true that \(\alpha_H^V(u)=\alpha_G^V(f(u))\).<tbc>

3. **Edge attributes are preserved:** For all \((u,v)\in E_H\) it is true that \(\alpha_H^E(u,v)=\alpha_G^E(f(u),f(v))\).

We write \(\#\mathrm{Hom}(H\rightarrow G)\) for the number of homomorphism from _H_ to _G_.

Next, we use homomorphism to define a witness function. Note that each input graph _G_ has a length constraint _B_.

**Definition of a Witness:**

• \(W=\{X|X\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{\ge 1}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\}\),<tbc>

• \(\mathrm{cost}(X)=\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot c\),<tbc>

• Let _P_ be a graph. We say that _P_ is a _X-colored s,t-path_ if<tbc>

– _P_ is a path with colored start-vertex _s_ and colored end-vertex _t_,<tbc>

– each edge in _P_ is colored with a color \((c,\ell)\), and<tbc>

**–** for each \((n,c,\ell)\in X\) the path _P_ contains exactly _n_ edges of color \((c,\ell)\).<tbc>

<tbc>Let _P<sub>X</sub>_:={_P|P_ is a _X_-colored _s,t_-path} be a set of paths then we define<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathrm{check}(G,X)=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
\sum_{P\in P_X}\#\mathrm{Hom}(P\rightarrow G) & \text{if}\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot\ell\le B \\
0 & \text{otherwise}
\end{array}\right.,\)<tbc>

<tbc>where _B_ is length constraint of _G_.

**Lemma 8.10.** _The triple_ \((W,\mathrm{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\mathrm{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) _is a witness function of OPT._

_Proof._ We start by showing that for all \(X\in W\) with \(\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot\ell\le B\) we obtain

\(\mathrm{check}(G,X)=\#\{\text{walks in}G\text{from}s\text{to}t\text{s.t. for all}(n,c,\ell)\in X\text{the color}(c,\ell)\text{is used}n\text{times}\}.\) (3)

Let \(P\in P_X\) be a path. Since _P_ is a _X_-colored _s,t_-path, we obtain that _V(P_)={_v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>t</sub>_} and _E(P_)={_e_<sub>1</sub>_,...e_<sub>_t_-1</sub>} with \(\alpha_P^V(v_1)=s\), \(\alpha_P^V(v_t)=t\) and \(\alpha_P^E(e_i)=(c_i,\ell_i)\). Now, \(\#\mathrm{Hom}(P\rightarrow G)\) is equal to the number of walks in _G_ that start at _s_, end at _t_, and where we used an edge of color \((c_i,\ell_i)\) during the _i_th step of the walk. Thus, equation (3) follows since check(_G,X_) computes the sum over all possible _X_-colored _s,t_-paths.

Next, we check that \((W,\mathrm{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\mathrm{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) is a witness function of _OPT_. For the first property, let \(G\in\mathcal{G}\), \(X\in W\) and assume that check(_G,X)\>_0. By (3), we obtain that there is walk from _s_ to _t_ that uses the colors _X_. This walk induces a path _P_ from _s_ to _t_ that is<tbc>

<tbc>obtained by deleting repeating vertices and edges of the walk. Note that for each \((n,c,\ell)\in X\) the path _P_ uses edges of color \((c,\ell)\) at most _n_ times. Further since check(_G,X)\>_0, we obtain

\(\ell(P)\le\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot\ell\le B\text{and}c(P)\le\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot c=\mathrm{cost}(X).\)

Thus, _P_ is a feasible path of length at most _B_. Further, \(OPT(G)\le\mathrm{cost}(X)\) since _P_ has cost at most cost(_X_).

Next, assume that \(OPT(G)<\infty\) then there is a _s,t_-path _P_<sup>∗</sup> with \(\ell(P^*)\le B\) and _OPT(G_)=_c(P_<sup>∗</sup>). Now, let _X_ be the set that contains \((n,c,\ell)\) if and only if the edge color \((c,\ell)\) is used _n_ times in _P_<sup>∗</sup>. Observe that \(\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot\ell=\ell(P^*)\le B\). Further note that \(OPT(G)=c(P^*)=\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot\ell=\mathrm{cost}(X)\). Since _P_<sup>∗</sup> is path _s,t_-path and therefore a walk, (3) yields that \(\mathrm{check}(G,X)\ge 1>0\). Thus, _OPT(G_)=cost(_X_) and check(_G,X)\>_0.

The proof of the following lemma was discussed in \[Bök19, Section 1.1\]. The lemma is a generalization of Theorem 1 in \[DGR18\].

**Lemma 8.11.** _Let F be a tree and H,G be two graphs. If_ \(H\equiv_{1\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}G\) _then_ \(\#\mathrm{Hom}(F\rightarrow G)=\#\mathrm{Hom}(F\rightarrow H)\).

**Lemma 8.12.** _The function_ \(\mathrm{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _is 1-WL invariant._

_Proof._ Let \(G,H\in\mathcal{G}\) be two graphs with \(G\equiv_{1\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}H\). According to Lemma 8.11, \(\#\mathrm{Hom}(F\rightarrow G)=\#\mathrm{Hom}(F\rightarrow H)\) for all trees _F_. Since every path is a tree, we obtain that check(_G,X_)=check(_H,X_) for all \(X\in W\) that satisfy the length constraint, that is, \(\sum_{(n,c,\ell)\in X}n\cdot\ell\le B\). Note that _G_ and _H_ have the same length constraint since \(G\equiv_{1\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}H\).

_Proof of Theorem 8.8._ According to Lemma 8.10, the triple \((W,\mathrm{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\mathrm{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) is a witness function of _OPT_. Further, Lemma 8.12 shows that check is 1-WL invariant. Thus, Lemma 8.7 implies that CSP is 1-WL invariant.

**Corollary 8.13.** _There is an algorithm that solves the_ CSP _problem with k prior instances each of size at most n in O(k(n+m_)log_n_) _preprocessing time and O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time._

_Proof._ This is a direct consequence of Theorem 8.4 combined with Theorem 8.8.

## 8.4 CST is 2-WL Invariant

Next, we again turn to the Constrained Spanning Tree (CST) problem. Recall that, in Theorem 6.3, we obtained a randomized algorithm in the Isomorphic-Priors model with \(\widetilde{O}(kn^\omega)\) preprocessing time and \(O(n^\omega)\) query time. In the following, we obtain a deterministic algorithm via 2-WL. Write _OPT_ for the optimal value function of CST and G for the set of valid input graphs of CST. We show that _OPT_ is 2-WL invariant for all values.<sup>27</sup> This together with Theorem 8.3 this immediately yields a deterministic algorithm for CST in the Isomorphic-Priors model.

**Theorem 8.14.** _The problem_ CST _is 2-WL invariant._

<sup>27</sup>As before, we say that two input graphs _G_ and _H_ are 2-WL equivalent if _G_ and _H_ have the same budget _B_ value and \(G\equiv_{2\text{-}\mathrm{WL}}H\) for the underlying attributed graphs.

## Definition of a Witness:

To prove Theorem 8.14 we define a witness for _OPT_ and show that this witness is 2-WL invariant.

• \(W=\{X|X\subseteq\mathbb{N}_{\ge 0}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\times\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\}\),<tbc>

• \(\mathrm{cost}(X)=\sum_{(n,c,d)\in X}n\cdot c\),<tbc>

• Let _T_ be a graph. We say that _T_ is a _X-colored tree_ if<tbc>

– _T_ is a tree where each vertex has the same color,<tbc>

– each edge in _T_ is colored with a color (_c,d_), and<tbc>

**–** for each \((n,c,d)\in X\) the tree _T_ contains exactly _n_ edges of color (_c,d_).<tbc>

<tbc>We define<tbc>

<tbc>\(\mathrm{check}(G,X)=\left|\left\{T:T\text{is a spanning tree of}G\text{and}T\text{is}X\text{-colored and}\sum_{(n,c,d)\in X}n\cdot d\le B\right\}\right|,\)<tbc>

<tbc>where _B_ is the budget associated with the input graph _G_. This means that check(_G,X_)=0, whenever _X_ is outside the budget constraint of _B_

**Lemma 8.15.** _The triple_ \((W,\mathrm{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\mathrm{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) _is a witness function of OPT._

_Proof._ Let \(G\in\mathcal{G}\) and \(X\in W\) and assume that check(_G,X)\>_0. By the definition of check(_G,X_), we obtain that there is _X_-colored spanning tree _T_ of _G_. For each \((n,c,d)\in X\), the tree _T_ uses edges of color (_c,d_) exactly _n_ times. Further, since check(_G,X)\>_0 we obtain

\(\ell(T)=\sum_{(n,c,d)\in X}n\cdot d\le B\text{and}c(T)=\sum_{(n,c,d)\in X}n\cdot c=\mathrm{cost}(X).\)

Thus, _T_ is a feasible tree of length at most _B_. Additionally, \(OPT(G)\le\mathrm{cost}(X)\) since _T_ has cost cost(_X_).

Next, assume that \(OPT(G)<\infty\). Now, there is a spanning tree _T_<sup>∗</sup> with \(\sum_{(n,c,d)\in X}n\cdot d\le B\) and _OPT(G_)=_c(T_<sup>∗</sup>). Let _X_ be the set that contains (_n,c,d_) if and only if the edge color (_c,d_) is used _n_ times in _T_<sup>∗</sup>. Note that \(OPT(G)=c(T^*)=\sum_{(n,c,d)\in X}n\cdot d=\mathrm{cost}(X)\). Since _T_<sup>∗</sup> is by definition a _X_-colored spanning tree, we obtain that check(_G,X)\>_0. Thus, _OPT_<sub>CST</sub>(_G_)=cost(_X_) and check(_G,X)\>_0.

We prove the following lemma which together with Lemma 8.15 immediately yields Theorem 8.14.

**Lemma 8.16.** _The function_ \(\mathrm{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) _is 2-WL invariant on_ G.

_Proof (sketch)._ To prove Lemma 8.16 we show that check(_G,X_)=check(_H,X_) for all \(G,H\in\mathcal{G}\) with \(G\equiv_{2\text{-WL}}H\) and \(X\in W\). Without loss of generality we assume that _X_ satisfies \(\sum_{(n,c,d)\in X}n\cdot d\le B\) since otherwise 0=check(_G,X_)=check(_H,X_)=0. We start with the Kirchhoff polynomial (see \[CY00\])

\(\mathrm{Kir}(G):=\sum_T\prod_{e\in T}X_e,\)

where each edge _e_ in _G_ has its own variable _X<sub>e</sub>_ and the sum is over all spanning trees _T_ of _G_. If we substituted each _X<sub>e</sub>_ with a new variable _c(e_), where _c(e_) is the color of the edge _e_, then we get the _Spanning Tree Polynomial P<sub>ST</sub>(G_) from Section 6.2. Formally, we have \(\mathrm{Kir}(G)|_{X_e=c(e)}\equiv P_{ST}(G)\), where Kir(_G_)|<sub>_X<sub>e</sub>=c(e_)</sub> is obtained by substituting _X<sub>e</sub>_ with _c(e_) in Kir(_G_).

Further, note that the function check(_G,X_) computes the coefficients of the _Spanning Tree Polynomial_. Specially, the coefficient _c_<sub>_w_<sub>1</sub>_,...w_<sub>_n_-1</sub></sub> of _P<sub>ST</sub>(G_) is equal to check(_G,X_) where _X_ is the set that contains a triple (_n,c,d_) if and only if the color (_c,d_) appears exactly _n_ times in the multiset {_w_<sub>1</sub>_,...w_<sub>_n_-1</sub>} (note that each _w<sub>i</sub>_ is actually a (_c,d_)-tuple). Thus, if \(P_{ST}(G)\equiv P_{ST}(H)\) then check(_G,X_)=check(_H,X_) for all \(X\in W\), proving the theorem.

To show \(P_{ST}(G)\equiv P_{ST}(H)\), we use a result from \[CY00\] which states that for each \(i\in[n]\)

\(\mathrm{Kir}(G)\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i(G)),\)

where \(\tilde{L}_i(G)\) is the Laplacian _L(G_) of _G_ with its _i_-th row and _i_-th column removed. Note that \(\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i(G))\) is a polynomial over the variables _X<sub>e</sub>_. Now, \(\mathrm{Kir}(G)|_{X_e=c(e)}\equiv P_{ST}(G)\) and \(\mathrm{Kir}(G)\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i(G))\) implies that \(P_{ST}(G)\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(G))\) where \(\tilde{L}_i^C(G)\) is obtained by substituted each variable _X<sub>e</sub>_ in \(\tilde{L}_i(G)\) with _c(e_).

Thus, it is enough to prove \(P_{ST}(G)\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(G))\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(H))\equiv P_{ST}(H)\) whenever \(H\equiv_{2\text{-WL}}G\). By \[RS23\]<sup>28</sup>, _L<sup>C</sup>(G_) is cospectral to _L<sup>C</sup>(H_). Let \(d_i^G\) (respectively \(d_i^H\)) be the _i_th coefficient of the characteristic polynomial of _L<sup>C</sup>(G_) (respectively _L<sup>C</sup>(H_)). Note that \(d_i^H,d_i^G\in\mathbb{C}[c(e)]\).<sup>29</sup> Since _L<sup>C</sup>(G_) and _L<sup>C</sup>(H_) are cospectral, it follows that \(d_i^H=d_i^G\). Note that \(d_1^H\) is the linear coefficient of the characteristic polynomial.<sup>30</sup> A well-known theorem from linear algebra (see e.g. \[Alf18, Theorem 1.8\]) implies<tbc>

\(d_1^H\equiv-\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(H)),d_1^G\equiv-\sum_{i=1}^n\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(G)).\)

<tbc>Now, since \(\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(H))\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_j^C(H))\) and \(\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(G))\equiv=\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_j^C(G))\) for all \(i,j\in[n]\), we obtain

\(P_{ST}(G)\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(G))\equiv\frac{-d_1^G}{n}\equiv\frac{-d_1^H}{n}\equiv\mathrm{det}(\tilde{L}_i^C(H))\equiv P_{ST}(H).\)

_Proof of Theorem 8.14._ Let \(B\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}\). According to Lemma 8.15, the triple \((W,\mathrm{check}:\mathcal{G}\times W\rightarrow\mathbb{R},\mathrm{cost}:W\rightarrow\mathbb{R})\) is a witness function of _OPT_. Further, Lemma 8.16 shows that check is 2-WL invariant on G. Thus, Lemma 8.7 implies that CSP is 2-WL invariant.

_Proof._ This is a direct consequence of Theorem 8.3 combined with Theorem 8.14.

## 8.5 Examples when Weisfeiler-Leman Fails

Given a graph _G_ of order _n_ and maximum degree \(k\ge 3\). In \[CFI92\] Cai, Fürer, and Immerman introduced the idea of CFI graphs. ## 9.2 Iso-Problems and Gl-Completeness

We introduce the promise problem Iso-\(\Pi\) and show properties that will be used in later sections to show hardness results in our model.

**Definition 9.8.** For a decision problem \(\Pi\), define the promise problem Iso-\(\Pi=(\mathsf{Iso}-\Pi_\mathrm{YES},\mathsf{Iso}-\Pi_\mathrm{NO})\) over pairs of instances (_I,J_) by

\(\mathrm{Iso}-\Pi_\mathrm{YES}:=\{(I,J)|I\in\Pi\wedge J\cong I\},\mathrm{Iso}-\Pi_\mathrm{NO}:=\{(I,J)|I\in\Pi\wedge J\notin\Pi\}.\)

The input is promised to lie in Iso-\(\Pi_\mathrm{YES}\cup\mathsf{Iso}-\Pi_\mathrm{NO}\).

We recall the definition of polynomial-time many-one reductions.

**Definition 9.9.** We say that there is a _polynomial-time many-one reduction_ from \(\Pi\) to \(\Pi'\) if there exist a polynomial-time computable function _f_ such that \(X\in\Pi\) if and only if \(f(X)\in\Pi\).

We say that \(\Pi\) is Gl-hard if there is a polynomial-time many-one reduction from Gl to \(\Pi\). We say that \(\Pi\) is Gl-complete if there \(\Pi\) is Gl-hard and there is a polynomial-time many-one reduction from \(\Pi\) to Gl.

We show that for \(\Pi=\mathsf{Gl}\), Iso-\(\Pi\) is just a reformulation of Gl.

**Lemma 9.10.** Iso-Gl _is_ Gl_-complete._

_Proof._ Recall that Iso-Gl is the promise problem on pairs (_I,J_) of Gl-instances such that \(I\in\mathsf{Gl}\) and either \(J\cong I\) (YES) or \(J\notin\mathsf{Gl}\) (NO).

### (1) Iso-\(\mathsf{Gl}\in\mathsf{Gl}\).

Given an input (_I,J_), where _I_=(_G_<sub>0</sub>_,G_<sub>1</sub>) and _J_=(_H_<sub>0</sub>_,H_<sub>1</sub>), run a Gl-test to decide whether \(I\cong J\), i.e. whether \(G_0\cong H_0\) and \(G_1\cong H_1\). If \(I\cong J\) output YES, otherwise output NO. This is correct under the promise: in a YES-instance we have \(J\cong I\), while in a promised instance with \(J\unknown\cong I\) we cannot be in Iso-Gl<sub>YES</sub>, hence must be in Iso-Gl<sub>NO</sub>.

### (2) Gl-hardness.

We give a polynomial-time many-one reduction from Gl to Iso-Gl. Given a Gl-instance _I_=(_G,H_), output the pair

\(f(G,H):=\big((G,G),(G,H)\big).\)

Note that \((G,G)\in\mathsf{Gl}\) always. If \(G\cong H\), then \((G,H)\cong(G,G)\), so \(f(G,H)\in\mathsf{Iso}-\mathsf{Gl}_\mathrm{YES}\). If \(G\unknown\cong H\), then \((G,H)\notin\mathsf{Gl}\), so \(f(G,H)\in\mathsf{Iso}-\mathsf{Gl}_\mathrm{NO}\). Hence _f_ is a valid reduction and \(\mathsf{Gl}\le_m\) Iso-Gl.

### Conclusion.

We have shown \(\text{Iso-}\mathsf{Gl}\in\mathsf{Gl}\) and \(\mathsf{Gl}\le_m\text{Iso-Gl}\), therefore Iso-Gl is Gl-complete.

We conclude this section by showing that the promise problem is at most as hard as Gl independent of the problem it is based on.

**Lemma 9.11.** _Let_ \(\Pi\) _be a decision problem. Then_ Iso-\(\Pi\) _is in_ Gl.

_Proof._ We give a polynomial-time many-one reduction from Iso-\(\Pi\) to Gl.

On input (_I,J_), output the pair (_I,J_) as an instance of Gl (i.e., the question whether \(I\cong J\)). This mapping is polynomial time.

We claim it is correct under the promise defining Iso-\(\Pi\). If \((I,J)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi_\mathrm{YES}\), then \(J\cong I\), hence (_I,J_) is a YES-instance of Gl. If \((I,J)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi_\mathrm{NO}\), then \(I\in\Pi\) and \(J\notin\Pi\). Therefore, deciding \((I,J)\in\mathsf{Gl}\) decides \((I,J)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi\), and thus Iso-\(\Pi\le_m\mathsf{Gl}\), i.e. Iso-\(\Pi\) is in Gl.

## 9.3 Isomorphism-Preserving Reductions

A tool we use to show the hardness is isomorphism-preserving reductions

**Definition 9.12.** We call a function _R_ that maps instances of \(\Pi\) to instances of \(\Pi'\) an _isomorphism- preserving reduction_ if:

• _R_ is polynomial time computable.<tbc>

• _R_ is _correct_, that is \(I\in\Pi\) is a YES-instance of \(\Pi\) if and only if _R(I_) is a YES-instance of \(\Pi'\).<tbc>

• _R_ is _isomorphism-preserving_, that is if \(I_1,I_2\in\Pi\) are isomorphic in \(\Pi\) then _R(I_<sub>1</sub>)_,R(I_<sub>2</sub>) are isomorphic in \(\Pi'\).

We write \(\Pi\le_p^\cong\Pi'\) if such a reduction exits. Further, we say that a problem \(\Pi'\) is Gl-hard if \(\mathsf{Gl}\le_p^\cong\Pi'\).

The property of isomorphism-preserving reductions is that they can be used to show Gl-hardness of promise problems.

**Lemma 9.13.** _Let_ \(\Pi\) _and_ \(\Pi'\) _be decision problems. If_ Iso-\(\Pi\) _is_ Gl_-hard and_ \(\Pi\le_p^\cong\Pi'\)_, then_ Iso-\(\Pi'\) _is_ Gl_-hard._

_Proof._ Since Iso-\(\Pi\) is Gl-hard, there exists a polynomial-time reduction \(g:\mathsf{Gl}\le_m\text{Iso-}\Pi\).

It therefore suffices to give a polynomial-time reduction \(f:\text{Iso-}\Pi\le_m\text{Iso-}\Pi'\).

Let (_I,J_) be an instance of Iso-\(\Pi\). Since \(\Pi\le_p^\cong\Pi'\), there exists an isomorphism-preserving many-one reduction _R_ from \(\Pi\) to \(\Pi'\). Define

\(f(I,J):=(R(I),R(J)).\)

We check that _f_ maps promised instances to promised instances and preserves YES/NO.

### YES case.

If \((I,J)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi_\mathrm{YES}\), then \(I\in\Pi\) and \(J\cong I\). By correctness, \(R(I)\in\Pi'\), and by isomorphism preservation, \(R(J)\cong R(I)\). Hence \(f(I,J)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi'_\mathrm{YES}\).

If \((I,J)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi_\text{NO}\), then \(I\in\Pi\) and \(J\notin\Pi\). By correctness of _R_, we have \(R(I)\in\Pi'\) and \(R(J)\notin\Pi'\). Hence \(f(I,J)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi'_\text{NO}\).

\(\mathsf{GI}\le_m\text{Iso-}\Pi\le_m\text{Iso-}\Pi',\)

Then \(\Psi\) preserves edges of type (1) (it preserves equality of coordinates) and of type (2) (since \(\psi_G,\psi_H\) preserve adjacency), hence \(K(G,H)\cong K(G',H')\). Also \(n=|V(G)|=|V(G')|\), so the parameter _k=n_ is preserved. Thus \(R(G,H)\cong R(G',H')\) as IS instances.

**Lemma 9.16.** GI \(\le_p^\cong\mathsf{SAT}\).

_Proof._ We define a polynomial-time, isomorphism-preserving many-one reduction from GI to SAT.

## Reduction.

Let (_G,H_) be an instance of GI. If \(|V(G)|\neq|V(H)|\), output a fixed unsatisfiable CNF (e.g. \((x)\wedge(\neg x)\)). Hence assume |_V(G_)|=|_V(H_)|=_n_.

Introduce Boolean variables

\(x_{u,v}\text{for each}u\in V(G),v\in V(H),\)

with the intended meaning "\(\varphi(u)=v\)".

We construct a CNF formula \(\Phi(G,H)\) consisting of the following clauses.

**Bijection constraints.**

1. _Each u maps somewhere:_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\vee_{v\in V(H)}x_{u,v}\text{for all}u\in V(G).\)<tbc>

2. _Each u maps to at most one v:_<tbc>

<tbc>\((\neg x_{u,v}\vee\neg x_{u,v^\prime})\text{for all}u\in V(G),v\neq v'\in V(H).\)<tbc>

3. _Injectivity (each v is used by at most one u):_<tbc>

<tbc>\((\neg x_{u,v}\vee\neg x_{u^\prime,v})\text{for all}v\in V(H),u\neq u'\in V(G).\)

## Adjacency consistency constraints.

For every pair of distinct vertices \(u,u'\in V(G)\) and distinct vertices \(v,v'\in V(H)\) such that<tbc>

\(\mathbf{1}[(u,u')\in E(G)]\oplus\mathbf{1}[(v,v')\in E(H)]=1,\)

<tbc>add the clause

\((\neg x_{u,v}\vee\neg x_{u^\prime,v^\prime}).\)

This construction is polynomial-time and yields a CNF formula of size polynomial in _n_.

## Correctness.

We show that \(\Phi(G,H)\) is satisfiable if and only if \(G\cong H\).

(\(\Rightarrow\)) Suppose \(\varphi:V(G)\rightarrow V(H)\) is an isomorphism. Set \(x_{u,\varphi(u)}=\) true for all \(u\in V(G)\) and all other variables to false. Then the bijection constraints are satisfied. For adjacency consistency, for any \(u\neq u'\) let \(v=\varphi(u)\) and \(v'=\varphi(u')\). Since \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism,

\((u,u')\in E(G)\Longleftrightarrow(v,v')\in E(H),\)

so the XOR condition is false and no adjacency-consistency clause is violated. Hence the assignment satisfies \(\Phi(G,H)\).

(\(\Leftarrow\)) Conversely, let _A_ satisfy \(\Phi(G,H)\). By constraints (1) and (2), for each \(u\in V(G)\) there is exactly one \(v\in V(H)\) with _A(x<sub>u,v</sub>_)= true; define \(\varphi(u)=v\). Constraint (3) implies that \(\varphi\) is injective, and since |_V(G_)|=|_V(H_)| it is a bijection. Now fix distinct \(u,u'\in V(G)\) and let \(v=\varphi(u)\), \(v'=\varphi(u')\). If exactly one of \((u,u')\in E(G)\) and \((v,v')\in E(H)\) holds, then the corresponding clause \((\neg x_{u,v}\vee\neg x_{u^\prime,v^\prime})\) would be falsified (both literals false), contradicting satisfaction. Therefore

\((u,u')\in E(G)\Longleftrightarrow(\varphi(u),\varphi(u'))\in E(H),\)

so \(\varphi\) is an isomorphism \(G\cong H\).

## Isomorphism preservation.

We take "isomorphism" between SAT instances to mean: there is a variable renaming (and clause permutation) mapping one CNF to the other. If \((G,H)\cong(G',H')\) as GI instances, there exist isomorphisms \(\psi_G:V(G)\rightarrow V(G')\) and \(\psi_H:V(H)\rightarrow V(H')\). Define the variable renaming \(\rho\) by

\(\rho(x_{u,v}):=x_{\psi_G(u),\psi_H(v)}.\)

Then \(\rho\) maps the three families of bijection constraints for (_G,H_) to the corresponding families for \((G',H')\), and it maps each adjacency-consistency clause to the corresponding clause in \(\Phi(G',H')\). Hence \(\Phi(G,H)\cong\Phi(G',H')\) as SAT instances, so the reduction is isomorphism-preserving.

Therefore \(\mathsf{GI}\le_p^\cong\mathsf{SAT}\).

**Lemma 9.17.** \(\mathsf{IS}\le_p^\cong\mathsf{MaxCut}\).

_Proof._ We use the standard gadget reduction from Independent Set to MaxCut from Barak’s online textbook \[Bar23\] and verify that it is also isomorphism-preserving.

#### Decision versions.

We view IS as the decision problem on instances (_G,k_) asking whether _G_ has an independent set of size at least _k_, and MaxCut as the decision problem on instances (_H,T_) asking whether _H_ has a cut of size at least _T_.

### Reduction.

Given an instance (_G,k_) of IS, let _G_=(_V,E_) and _m_:=|_E_|. We construct a graph _H=R(G_) as follows (cf. \[Bar23\]): add a distinguished vertex _s<sup>⋆</sup>_ adjacent to every \(v\in V\) ; and for each edge \(e=\{u,v\}\in E\), attach a constant-size gadget by adding two new vertices _e<sub>u</sub>,e<sub>v</sub>_ and the five edges<tbc>

\(\{e_u,e_v\},\{s^\star,e_u\},\{s^\star,e_v\},\{u,e_u\},\{v,e_v\}.\)

<tbc>(No other edges are added; in particular, we do not keep the original edges of _G_ in _H_.) We set the MaxCut threshold to

\(T:=k+4m,\)

and output the instance (_H,T_). Barak proves that _G_ has an independent set of size at least _k_ if and only if _H_ has a cut of size at least _T_, so this is a valid polynomial-time many-one reduction \[Bar23\].

### Isomorphism preservation.

Let \(\varphi:G\rightarrow G'\) be a graph isomorphism and note that it preserves the parameter _k_ and the number of edges _m_. We extend \(\varphi\) to an isomorphism \(\psi:R(G)\rightarrow R(G')\) by mapping \(s^\star\mapsto s^\star\), each original vertex \(u\mapsto\varphi(u)\), and for each edge \(e=\{u,v\}\in E(G)\) mapping the gadget vertices \(e_u\mapsto(\varphi(e))_{\varphi(u)}\) and \(e_v\mapsto(\varphi(e))_{\varphi(v)}\), where \(\varphi(e)=\{\varphi(u),\varphi(v)\}\in E(G')\). Since the gadget adjacencies are defined purely in terms of incidences to _s<sup>⋆</sup>_, _u_, _v_, and the internal gadget edge {_e<sub>u</sub>,e<sub>v</sub>_}, this mapping preserves all edges. Hence \(R(G)\cong R(G')\) and the threshold _T_ is preserved.

Therefore the reduction is isomorphism-preserving, i.e. \(\mathsf{IS}\le_p^\cong\mathsf{MaxCut}\).

## 9.5 Hardness in the Isomorphism-Priors Model

We show that the Gl-hardness of Iso-\(\Pi\) implies that \(\Pi\) cannot be solved in our model with fast preprocessing, unless \(\mathsf{Gl}\in\mathsf{P}\).

**Lemma 9.24.** _Let_ \(\Pi\) _be a decision problem such that_ Iso-\(\Pi\) _is_ Gl_-hard. Unless_ \(\mathsf{Gl}\in\mathsf{P}\), \(\Pi\) _cannot be solved inside the Isomorphic-Priors model with k prior instances each of size at most n with preprocessing and query time polynomial in n, even when k_=1 _prior instance is given._

_Proof._ Assume that there exists an algorithm for \(\Pi\) in the Isomorphic-Priors model with preprocessing time poly_<sub>k</sub>(n_) and query time poly_<sub>k</sub>(n_), and that it is correct on all valid queries. In particular, consider the case _k_=1.

We show that this implies Iso-\(\Pi\in\mathsf{P}\). Given an input (_G,H_) to Iso-\(\Pi\), run the model’s preprocessing phase on the single prior instance _G_ together with \(L=\Pi(G)\) (i.e., _L_=1 if any only if _G_ is a YES-instances), obtaining a data structure _D_. Then query the model on _H_ and obtain an output

\(z:=\mathsf{Query}(D,H)\in\{0,1,\perp\}.\)

We decide Iso-\(\Pi\) by outputting YES iff _z_=1, and NO otherwise (in particular, treat \(z=\perp\) as NO). Correctness holds under the promise defining Iso-\(\Pi\):

• If \((G,H)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi_\mathrm{YES}\), then \(G\in\Pi\) and \(H\cong G\). Since \(\Pi\) is invariant under isomorphism, \(\Pi(H)=\Pi(G)=1\), so the model must output \(z=\Pi(H)=1\), and we accept.<tbc>

• If \((G,H)\in\text{Iso-}\Pi_\mathrm{NO}\), then \(G\in\Pi\) and \(H\notin\Pi\), i.e. \(\Pi(H)=0\). By correctness of the model algorithm on non-matching queries, on input _H_ it outputs either \(z=\Pi(H)=0\) or the special symbol \(\perp\). In both cases we reject.

The running time is polynomial, since preprocessing on one instance and one query are polynomial in _n_.

Thus Iso-\(\Pi\in\mathsf{P}\). Since by assumption Iso-\(\Pi\) is Gl-hard, this implies \(\mathsf{Gl}\in\mathsf{P}\). Therefore, unless \(\mathsf{Gl}\in\mathsf{P}\), no such algorithm exists for \(\Pi\) in the Isomorphic-Priors model (even for _k_=1).

We show that a problem, that can be reduced to Gl with an isomorphism-preserving reduction, cannot be solved in our model with a small data structure, unless \(\mathsf{Gl}\in\mathsf{coMA}\).
