## 9.6 Proof of Hardness for Gap-Max-_k_-Coverage

In this section, we show that Max-_k_-Coverage cannot be approximated better than (1-1_/e_) in our model, unless Max 3-SAT can be approximated arbitrarily well in our model. We achieve this by first observing that Feige’s _k_-prover system works for general Max 3-SAT and is not limited to bounded-occurrences. This is necessary because bounded occurrences would imply that the underlying isomorphism problem can be solved fast. We then go on and show that this implies a isomorphism-preserving reduction.

**Lemma 9.26** (Feige’s _k_-prover system for general Max 3-SAT)**.** _Consider the k-prover proof system of Section 2.3 in \[Fei98\] applied to an arbitrary 3CNF formula_ \(\phi\) _(no bounded-occurrence assumption). Let_ \(\varepsilon\in(0,1)\).

<sup>38</sup>That is, _L_=1 if \(G_1\cong G_2\) and zero, otherwise. <sup>39</sup>Here, \(\Pi(x)=1\) if \(x\in\Pi\) and zero otherwise.

1. _If_ \(\phi\) _is satisfiable, then there is a prover strategy that causes the verifier to always_ strongly _accept._<tbc>

_2._ _If_ \(OPT(\phi)\le 1-\varepsilon\) _(i.e., no assignment satisfies more than a_ \((1-\varepsilon)\)_-fraction of clauses), then the verifier_ weakly _accepts with probability at most_ \(k^2\cdot 2^{-c\ell}\)_, where c\>_0 _depends only on_ \(\varepsilon\) _(and on the constant answer length), and_ \(\ell\) _is the repetition parameter of the verifier._

_Proof._ The verifier samples \(\ell\) clauses uniformly and independently and chooses one distinguished variable per clause, exactly as in \[Fei98, Sec. 2.3\]. The weak predicate is "some pair of provers is consistent" (on the induced assignment to the \(\ell\) distinguished-variable positions), and the strong predicate is "every pair is consistent" \[Fei98, Sec. 2.3\].

## Completeness.

If \(\phi\) is satisfiable, fix any satisfying assignment and let every prover answer consistently with it. Then the induced assignments to the distinguished-variable positions are identical for all provers, so the verifier always strongly accepts (identical to Feige’s argument) \[Fei98, Lem. 2.3.1\].

## Soundness: reducing to two provers and parallel repetition.

Assume \(OPT(\phi)\le 1-\varepsilon\) and suppose the verifier weakly accepts with probability at least \(\delta\). Then there exist two provers whose answers are consistent with probability at least \(\delta/k^2\) (by averaging over the \(\genfrac(){pt}{2}{k}{2}\) pairs), exactly as in Feige \[Fei98, Lem. 2.3.1\]. By the Hamming-distance property of the code used to distribute queries, there are at least \(\ell/6\) coordinates in which one of these provers receives a clause and the other receives the distinguished variable from that clause (again exactly as in Feige) \[Fei98, Lem. 2.3.1\]. Fix the questions on the remaining \(5\ell/6\) coordinates to maximize acceptance; the acceptance probability remains at least \(\delta/k^2\). Now ignore those fixed coordinates. This yields a strategy for a two-prover system that succeeds with probability at least \(\delta/k^2\) on \(\ell/6\) independent coordinates, i.e., on \(\ell/6\) parallel repetitions of the underlying two-prover test.

## Base two-prover error does not need bounded occurrence.

Feige’s Proposition 2.2.1 (stated for 3CNF-5) bounds the optimal acceptance probability of the base two-prover test by \(1-\varepsilon/3\) when at most a \((1-\varepsilon)\)-fraction of clauses are simultaneously satisfiable \[Fei98, Prop. 2.2.1\]. Its proof uses only: (i) the second prover’s strategy induces a global assignment _x_, (ii) a random clause is unsatisfied by _x_ with probability at least \(\varepsilon\), and (iii) conditioned on such a clause, if the first prover makes it satisfied by changing at least one literal, then a uniformly random distinguished variable from that clause disagrees with probability at least 1/3. This argument does not depend on how many times a variable appears in the formula (variables may occur unboundedly often).

Hence the base two-prover system has constant error at most \(1-\varepsilon/3\), independent of _n_ and of occurrence bounds.

## Parallel repetition.

By Raz’s parallel repetition theorem (Feige’s Theorem 2.2.2), repeating a one-round two-prover system _t_ times independently in parallel reduces the acceptance probability to at most 2<sup>-_ct_</sup> for some constant _c\>_0 that depends only on the base error and the constant answer length \[Fei98, Thm. 2.2.2\]. Taking \(t=\ell/6\), we obtain

\(\delta/k^2\le 2^{-c\ell},\)

after renaming constants, and thus \(\delta\le k^2\cdot 2^{-c\ell}\).

This proves the claimed soundness bound for arbitrary 3CNF formulas, without any bounded- occurrence assumption.

This _k_-prover systems can be used for an isomorphism-preserving reduction.

**Lemma 9.27.** _For every_ \(\varepsilon,\varepsilon'\in(0,1/3)\)_, there is an isomorphism-preserving reduction_

\(\mathsf{Gap}\text{-Max-3-SAT}_{1,1-\varepsilon}\le_p^\cong\mathsf{Gap}\text{-Max-}k\text{-Coverage}_{1,1-1/e+\varepsilon^\prime}.\)

_Proof._ Fix \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/3)\). We construct an isomorphism-preserving mapping from 3CNF formulas to Max-_k_-Coverage instances, following Feige \[Fei98\], and use Lemma 9.26 (Feige’s Lemma 2.3.1 without bounded-occurrence) as the only nontrivial black box about the underlying _k_-prover system.

## No regularization.

We do _not_ apply any bounded-occurrence / regularization preprocessing: such steps typically require non-canonical choices (e.g., ordering occurrences), and are therefore not isomorphism-preserving in general.

## Step 1: The reduction \(\Phi\mapsto(U(\Phi),\mathcal{S}(\Phi),k')\).

Let \(\Phi\) be a 3CNF instance. Consider the _k_-prover verifier from \[Fei98, Sec. 2.3\] with repetition parameter \(\ell\) (to be chosen later as a function of \(\varepsilon\)). Let R be the set of random strings of the verifier; write _R_:=|R|. For each \(r\in\mathcal{R}\), the verifier determines (for each prover \(i\in[k]\)) a question _q<sub>i</sub>(r_) (a tuple of clause/variable identifiers as in \[Fei98, Sec. 2.3\]). Let _Q_ be the number of possible questions a prover can receive (as in Feige).

_Partition systems._ Fix parameters (_m,L,k,d_) as in Feige’s partition-system lemma (Lemma 3.2 in \[Fei98\]), with \(L=2^\ell\). For each \(r\in\mathcal{R}\), create an independent copy of the partition system<tbc>

\(B_r:=B(m,L,k,d)\)

<tbc>on a ground set of size _m_, equipped with _L_ partitions indexed by strings \(p\in\{0,1\}^\ell\). Each such partition consists of _k_ disjoint parts, which we denote<tbc>

\(\mathcal{P}_{r,p}=\big\{B(r,p,1),\dots,B(r,p,k)\big\},\bigcup_{i=1}^kB(r,p,i)=B_r.\)

<tbc>_Universe._ Define the universe as the disjoint union of all these ground sets:

\(U(\Phi):=\unknown_{r\in\mathcal{R}}\big(\{r\}\times B_r\big),\)

so \(|U(\Phi)|=mR\).

_Sets._ For each prover \(i\in[k]\), each question _q_ that prover _i_ may receive, and each possible answer _a_ to that question, define a set \(S(q,a,i)\subseteq U(\Phi)\) by<tbc>

\(S(q,a,i):=\bigcup_{r\in\mathcal{R}:q_i(r)=q}\big(\{r\}\times B(r,p_r(a),i)\big),\)

<tbc>where \(p_r(a)\in\{0,1\}^\ell\) is the induced assignment to the \(\ell\) distinguished variables selected under randomness _r_ (exactly as in Feige’s reduction). Let<tbc>

\(\mathcal{S}(\Phi):=\big\{S(q,a,i):i\in[k],q\in\mathcal{Q}_i,a\in\mathcal{A}_{i,q}\big\}.\)

<tbc>_Budget._ Set

\(k':=k^Q,\)

corresponding to choosing, for each prover, one answer for each of its _Q_ possible questions (as in Feige’s Max-_k_-Cover hardness, Section 5 of \[Fei98\]).

We output the Max-_k_-Coverage instance<tbc>

\(R(\Phi):=\big(U(\Phi),\mathcal{S}(\Phi),k'\big).\)

## Step 2: Gap correctness (black-box).

We argue informally, following Feige.

_YES case._ If \(OPT(\Phi)=1\), then by Lemma 9.26 there is a prover strategy that causes the verifier to _strongly_ accept on every random string. Fix that strategy and choose the \(k'\) sets that correspond to the provers’ answers on all possible questions (one answer per question per prover, hence _k<sup>Q</sup>_ choices total). For each _r_, strong acceptance implies that the induced strings \(p_r(\cdot)\) are consistent across provers, and therefore the chosen sets cover, inside the block \(\{r\}\times B_r\), all _m_ points (because the _k_ parts of P_<sub>r,p</sub>_ partition _B<sub>r</sub>_). Hence the chosen \(k'\) sets cover all of \(U(\Phi)\), so \(OPT(R(\Phi))=1\).

_NO case._ If \(OPT(\Phi)\le 1-\varepsilon\), then by Lemma 9.26 the verifier weakly accepts with probability at most \(\delta\), where \(\delta\) can be made exponentially small in \(\ell\). Feige’s analysis of the reduction (using the partition-system lemma) shows that any family of \(k'\) sets corresponds to a (possibly inconsistent) prover strategy, and that the fraction of universe elements covered is at most \(1-1/e+O(\delta)+O(1/d)\) (cf. \[Fei98, Sec. 4-5\]). Choosing \(\ell\) and _d_ large enough as functions of \(\varepsilon\) makes the additive terms \(O(\delta)+O(1/d)\) arbitrarily small; in particular, we can choose parameters so that the covered fraction is at most \(1-1/e+\varepsilon'\). Therefore \(OPT(R(\Phi))\le 1-1/e+\varepsilon'\) in the NO case.

Altogether, \(\Phi\in\mathsf{Gap}\mathsf{Max}\mathsf{3}\mathsf{SAT}_{1,1-\varepsilon^\prime}\) implies \(R(\Phi)\in\mathsf{Gap}\mathsf{Max}\mathsf{3}\mathsf{Coverage}_{1,1-1/e+\varepsilon^\prime}\).

## Step 3: Isomorphism preservation.

Let \(\alpha:\Phi\rightarrow\Phi'\) be an isomorphism of 3CNF instances (renaming variables and permuting clauses, preserving literal signs). We build an isomorphism between \(R(\Phi)=(U,\mathcal{S},k')\) and \(R(\Phi')=(U',\mathcal{S}',k')\).

The verifier’s random string \(r\in\mathcal{R}\) specifies a pattern of queries (which clause indices are chosen, which variables are distinguished, etc.). Under \(\alpha\), clause/variable identifiers are renamed, and hence each question _q_ and answer _a_ is renamed canonically to \(\alpha(q)\) and \(\alpha(a)\). Define a bijection \(\beta_U:U\rightarrow U'\) by<tbc>

\(\beta_U(r,x):=(r,x)\text{for}x\in B_r,\)

<tbc>i.e. we keep the partition-system point and randomness index, but interpret the clause/variable identifiers inside the indexing data via \(\alpha\) (equivalently: we identify R across \(\Phi\) and \(\Phi'\) by the same randomness and query pattern, differing only by renamed identifiers). Define a bijection \(\beta_\mathcal{S}:\mathcal{S}\rightarrow\mathcal{S}'\) by<tbc>

\(\beta_\mathcal{S}\big(S(q,a,i)\big):=S(\alpha(q),\alpha(a),i).\)

<tbc>By construction, for every universe element (_r,x_) and every set _S(q,a,i_), we have

\((r,x)\in S(q,a,i)\Longleftrightarrow(r,x)\in S(\alpha(q),\alpha(a),i),\)

because membership is defined solely by (i) whether _q<sub>i</sub>(r_)=_q_ and (ii) which part _B(r,p<sub>r</sub>(a),i_) is selected, and both are invariant under renaming clause/variable identifiers. Hence \((\beta_U,\beta_\mathcal{S})\) preserves incidence, so it is an isomorphism of set systems. Therefore \(R(\Phi)\cong R(\Phi')\).

The mapping \(\Phi\mapsto R(\Phi)\) is polynomial-time, isomorphism-preserving, and maps YES-instances of \(\mathsf{Gap}\mathsf{Max}\mathsf{3}\mathsf{SAT}_{1,1-\varepsilon}\) to YES-instances of \(\mathsf{Gap}\mathsf{Max}\mathsf{3}\mathsf{Coverage}_{1,1-1/e+\varepsilon^\prime}\) and NO- instances to NO-instances of \(\mathsf{Gap}\mathsf{Max}\mathsf{3}\mathsf{Coverage}_{1,1-1/e+\varepsilon^\prime}\). ### 10.2 _k_-Clique Hypothesis and Consequence

One of the foundational hypotheses in fine-grained complexity \[Vas18\] states that, for every fixed integer \(k\ge 3\), no randomized algorithm can detect a _k_-clique in an _n_-vertex graph in \(O(n^\frac{\omega k}{3}-\epsilon)\) time for any constant \(\epsilon>0\). It is natural to ask whether this fundamental computational barrier translates to the Isomorphic-Priors model. We observe that if this hypothesis extends to our setting, then Graph Isomorphism is not polynomial-time solvable.

Recall our hypothesis from earlier:

**Hypothesis 3.1.** _(Isomorphic-Priors k_**-Clique _Hypothesis) For every fixed integer_ \(k\ge 3\) _and constant_ \(\epsilon>0\)_, no isomorphic-priors algorithm can detect a k-clique in an n-vertex graph with both preprocessing and query times_ \(O(n^{\omega k/3-\epsilon})\)_, even with O_(1) _prior graphs._

**Observation 10.1.** _Under Hypothesis 3.1,_ Graph Isomorphism _cannot be solved in polynomial time (i.e._ \(\mathsf{GI}\notin\mathsf{P}\)_)._

_Proof sketch._ Assume for contradiction that Graph Isomorphism can be solved in _O(n<sup>b</sup>_) time for some constant \(b\ge 1\). Let \(k=\lceil 10b\rceil\). We construct an isomorphic-priors algorithm for _k_-Clique to handle _O_(1) prior graphs that requires _O_(1) preprocessing time and _O(n<sup>b</sup>_) query time.

During preprocessing, the algorithm does nothing. Upon receiving a query graph _H_, it simply runs the _O(n<sup>b</sup>_)-time GI algorithm to test whether \(H\cong G_i\) for any _i_. If such _G<sub>i</sub>_ exists, it outputs the precomputed answer _OPT(G<sub>i</sub>_); otherwise, it correctly declares \(H\unknown\cong G_i\) for any _i_. This satisfies the correctness guarantees of the Isomorphic-Priors model.

Since we chose \(k=\lceil 10b\rceil\), our query time is _O(n<sup>b</sup>_)=_O(n_<sup>_k/_10</sup>). Because the matrix multiplication exponent \(\omega\ge 2\), we have \(\frac{\omega k}{3}\ge\frac{2k}{3}\) . Since \(k=\lceil 10b\rceil\ge 10\), _n_<sup>_k/_10</sup> is asymptotically faster than \(O(n^\frac{\omega k}{3}-0.001)\). This implies we can solve _k_-Clique in our model in \(O(n^\frac{\omega k}{3}-0.001)\) time, which contradicts Hypothesis 3.1.

Note that the implication \(\mathsf{GI}\notin\mathsf{P}\) in the observation above remains true under weaker variants of the hypothesis, specifically as long as _k_-Clique requires \(\Omega(n^{f(k)})\) time in our model for any monotonically increasing, unbounded function _f(k_). Consequently, refuting Hypothesis 3.1 would serve as an intermediate step toward a polynomial-time algorithm for Graph Isomorphism. Conversely, resolving the hypothesis, or any of its weaker variants, in the affirmative would prove that no such algorithm exists (i.e., \(\mathsf{GI}\notin\mathsf{P}\)).

## A Further Problems that are Invariant under 1-WL

We first provide the deferred proof of Lemma 7.14 concerning color-consistent strategies for Energy Game. We then give further examples of problems that are invariant under 1-WL and can therefore be solved in near-linear time in the Isomorphic-Priors model.

### A.1 Color-Consistent Strategies for Energy Game

_Proof of Lemma 7.14._ Let _h(v_) be the minimum initial energy required to win from _v_. By assumption, \(\sigma\) wins from every starting vertex _v_ with initial energy _h(v_). The shadow-play argument using Neighborhood Preservation in the proof of Theorem 7.12 shows that vertices of the same stable 1-WL color have the same minimum initial energy. Thus _h_ is constant on each color class.

For each color class _C_, choose an arbitrary representative \(r_C\in C\) and define _H(C_):=_h(r<sub>C</sub>_). For each stable color class \(C\subseteq V_1\) and each \(u\in C\), choose

\(\widehat{\sigma}(u)\in\big\{v\in V\big|(u,v)\in E,w(u,v)=w(r_C,\sigma(r_C)),\chi_\infty^G(v)=\chi_\infty^G(\sigma(r_C))\big\}.\)

This set is nonempty by Neighborhood Preservation.

Let \((u,v)\in E\) be an edge consistent with \(\widehat{\sigma}\), meaning that either \(u\in V_2\) or \(v=\widehat{\sigma}(u)\). Denote \(C=\chi_\infty^G(u)\) and \(D=\chi_\infty^G(v)\). There exists a \(\sigma\)-consistent edge (_r<sub>C</sub>,z_) with _w(r<sub>C</sub>,z_)=_w(u,v_) and<tbc>

\(\chi_\infty^G(z)=D\): for \(u\in V_1\), take \(z=\sigma(r_C)\); for \(u\in V_2\), use Neighborhood Preservation. Since \(\sigma\) wins from _r<sub>C</sub>_ with energy _H(C_), we have \(h(r_C)+w(u,v)\ge h(z)\) and therefore \(w(u,v)\ge H(D)-H(C)\).

Now fix any initial vertex _v_<sub>0</sub> and energy \(E_0\ge h(v_0)\), and consider any resulting infinite walk \(\pi=v_0v_1v_2\dots\) consistent with \(\widehat{\sigma}\). Applying the preceding inequality to each edge (_v<sub>k</sub>,v_<sub>_k_+1</sub>) yields a telescoping sum

\(E_k=E_0+\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}w(v_j,v_{j+1})\ge H(\chi_\infty^G(v_k))\ge 0\text{for all}k\ge 0.\)

Hence \(\widehat{\sigma}\) is optimal from every starting vertex and has the required consistency property. The construction of \(\widehat{\sigma}\) takes linear time.

## A.2 More Games on Graphs

We have shown in Section 7 that Energy Game can be solved efficiently in the Isomorphic-Priors model using the 1-WL algorithm. In the following, we extend them to more general games.

**Definition A.1** (Value-determined Game)**.** An instance of Value-determined Game is defined by a tuple \(G=(V,E,V_1,V_2,V_r,\delta,w,v_0,W,p)\), where

• (_V,E_) is a finite directed graph with no terminal states,<tbc>

• (_V_<sub>1</sub>_,V_<sub>2</sub>_,V<sub>r</sub>_) is a partition of _V_ , where Player 1 controls _V_<sub>1</sub>, Player 2 controls _V_<sub>2</sub>, and _V<sub>r</sub>_ are random nodes,<tbc>

• \(\delta\) is a transition probability function for random nodes: for each \(u\in V_r\), \(\delta(u)\) is a probability distribution over \(Succ(u)=\{v|(u,v)\in E\}\).<tbc>

• \(w:V\rightarrow\Sigma\) is a label function.<tbc>

• _v_<sub>0</sub> is the designated initial vertex.<tbc>

• \(W\subseteq\Sigma^\omega\) is the Borel objective for Player 1.<tbc>

• \(p\in[0,1]\) is a probability threshold.

A play \(\pi=v_0v_1v_2\dots\) is formed by moving a token: at step \(k\ge 0\), if \(v_k\in V_i,i\in\{1,2\}\), Player _i_ chooses an outgoing edge \((v_k,v_{k+1})\in E\) and moves the token to _v_<sub>_k_+1</sub>; if \(v_k\in V_r\), then the arena samples a node _v_<sub>_k_+1</sub> from \(\delta(v_k)\), and moves the token to _v_<sub>_k_+1</sub>. We slightly abuse the label function by denoting \(w(\pi):=w(v_0)w(v_1)w(v_2)\dots\). We denote \(\pi(\sigma,\tau)\) as the (randomized) play where Player 1 uses strategy \(\sigma\) and Player 2 uses strategy \(\tau\). We say

• Player 1 wins the game from _v_<sub>0</sub> if \(sup_\sigma inf_\tau Pr(w(\pi(\sigma,\tau))\in W)\ge p\),<tbc>

• Player 2 wins the game from _v_<sub>0</sub> if \(inf_\tau sup_\sigma Pr(w(\pi(\sigma,\tau))\in W)<p\).

The game is value-determined, if \(sup_\sigma inf_\tau Pr(w(\pi(\sigma,\tau))\in W)=inf_\tau sup_\sigma Pr(w(\pi(\sigma,\tau))\in W)\), which means that exactly one of the Players wins. For a value-determined game _G_, we define _OPT(G_)=YES if Player 1 wins from _v_<sub>0</sub>, and _OPT(G_)=NO otherwise.

We view a value-determined game as an attributed directed graph in the sense of Section 5. All instance-specific information can be encoded using vertex and edge attributes. In particular, the threshold _p_, which is a global parameter of the instance, can be encoded by including _p_ in the attribute of every vertex. We regard the Borel objective _W_ as a fixed global parameter. Thus, Value-determined Game fits the model of 5.

**Theorem A.2** (Value-Determined Game in the Isomorphic-Priors Model)**.** _There is an algorithm that solves the Value-determined Game problem with k prior instances each having at most n vertices and m edges in O(k(n+m_)log_n_) _preprocessing time and O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time._

Similar to solving Energy Game in the Isomorphic-Priors setting, we only need to show that if two games are 1-WL equivalent, then the winning player is the same.

We initialize 1-WL with the vertex types and labels, and use transition probabilities as labels on edges leaving random nodes. All other edges receive a distinguished dummy label. Colors are compared using a common refinement scheme. Strategies may be history-dependent and randomized.

**Theorem A.3.** _Let G and_ \(G'\) _be two instances of Value-determined Games with the same Borel objective W. If_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G'\) _and_ \(\chi_\infty^G(v_0)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_0)\)_, then the winners of G and_ \(G'\) _are the same._

_Proof._ By symmetry, it suffices to show that the value of \(G'\) is at least the value of _G_. Fix an arbitrary strategy \(\sigma\) for Player 1 in _G_. For simplicity, we use _w_ for the label functions of both games.

For every pair of equally colored vertices \(u,u'\), fix a color-preserving bijection \(b_{u,u^\prime}:\mathrm{Succ}(u)\rightarrow\mathrm{Succ}(u')\). At random nodes, additionally require \(\delta(u)(v)=\delta'(u')\big(b_{u,u^\prime}(v)\big)\). Such bijections exist by Neighborhood Preservation, since the refinement also includes transition probabilities as edge labels.

Fix a common infinite random tape, viewed as a sequence \((U_k)_{k\ge 0}\) of independent uniform random variables on \[0,1\], independent of the players’ randomization. At corresponding random nodes \(u,u'\), order the successors of _u_ arbitrarily and order those of \(u'\) according to \(b_{u,u^\prime}\). At step _k_, both games use _U<sub>k</sub>_ to sample from the corresponding cumulative probability intervals. The two transitions then have the correct marginal distributions and lead to successors matched by \(b_{u,u^\prime}\). This random tape is used only for the coupling and is not observed by the players.

We define \(\sigma'\) dynamically by maintaining a simulated "shadow play" in _G_. Let the current finite prefix of a play in \(G'\) be \(\pi'=(v'_0,v'_1,\dots,v'_k)\) and the shadow play in _G_ be \(\pi=(v_0,v_1,\dots,v_k)\). We show by induction on _k_ that \(\chi_\infty^G(v_i)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_i)\) for all \(i\le k\).

_Base case._ For _k_=0, the claim holds by assumption.

_Inductive step._ Assume the claim holds for all \(i\le k\). Since \(v'_k\) and _v<sub>k</sub>_ have the same color, they have the same vertex type.

• If _v<sub>k</sub>_ and \(v'_k\) are Player 1 nodes, we first move the token in _G_: the strategy \(\sigma\) selects a successor _v_<sub>_k_+1</sub> according to \(\sigma(\pi)\). Then we move the token in \(G'\) to \(v'_{k+1}=b_{v_k,v_k^\prime}(v_{k+1})\). By the choice of the bijection, \(\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_{k+1})=\chi_\infty^G(v_{k+1})\).<tbc>

• If _v<sub>k</sub>_ and \(v'_k\) are Player 2 nodes, we first move the token in \(G'\): Player 2 selects an arbitrary successor \(v'_{k+1}\) of \(v'_k\). We then move the token in _G_ to \(v_{k+1}=b_{v_k,v_k^\prime}^{-1}(v'_{k+1})\). Again, \(\chi_\infty^G(v_{k+1})=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_{k+1})\).<tbc>

• If _v<sub>k</sub>_ and \(v'_k\) are random nodes, the arena samples \(v'_{k+1}\sim\delta'(v'_k)\). Upon observing \(v'_{k+1}\), the strategy \(\sigma'\) appends to the shadow play the vertex \(v_{k+1}:=b_{v_k,v_k^\prime}^{-1}(v'_{k+1})\). This implements the coupling above: since \(\delta'(v'_k)(b_{v_k,v_k^\prime}(u))=\delta(v_k)(u)\) for every \(u\in\mathrm{Succ}(v_k)\), the induced shadow transition has distribution \(\delta(v_k)\). Moreover, color preservation gives \(\chi_\infty^G(v_{k+1})=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(v'_{k+1})\). Thus \(\sigma'\) reconstructs the shadow move from the observed move in \(G'\), without observing the random tape.

The fixed local bijections give a bijection between finite histories in the two games. Both directions of this correspondence depend only on the histories already observed. Therefore, \(\sigma'\) is a legal history-dependent strategy.

Now fix an arbitrary strategy \(\tau'\) for Player 2 in \(G'\). Using the history correspondence, define a strategy \(\tau\) in _G_ by transporting the choices of \(\tau'\) through the inverse local bijections. This is also a legal history-dependent strategy.

Under these strategy pairs, corresponding finite histories have equal probabilities. At player nodes, this follows from the construction of the strategies; at random nodes, it follows from the probability-preserving coupling. Recall that colors determine the labels of the nodes along a play. Thus the two games induce the same distribution on label sequences, and<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Pr}\big(w(\pi'(\sigma',\tau'))\in W\big)=\mathrm{Pr}\big(w(\pi(\sigma,\tau))\in W\big).\)

<tbc>Here \(\pi(\sigma,\tau)\) and \(\pi'(\sigma',\tau')\) denote the resulting infinite plays in _G_ and \(G'\), respectively.

Since this holds for every \(\tau'\), we have<tbc>

\(\mathrm{inf}_{\tau^\prime}\mathrm{Pr}\big(w(\pi'(\sigma',\tau'))\in W\big)\ge\mathrm{inf}_\tau\mathrm{Pr}\big(w(\pi(\sigma,\tau))\in W\big).\)

<tbc>Since \(\sigma\) was arbitrary, it follows that

\(\mathrm{sup}_{\sigma^\prime}\mathrm{inf}_{\tau^\prime}\mathrm{Pr}\big(w(\pi'(\sigma',\tau'))\in W\big)\ge\mathrm{sup}_\sigma\mathrm{inf}_\tau\mathrm{Pr}\big(w(\pi(\sigma,\tau))\in W\big).\)

By symmetry, the values of _G_ and \(G'\) are equal. Since both games are value-determined and have the same threshold _p_, their winners are the same.

_Proof of Theorem A.2._ The first part follows directly from Theorems A.3 and 8.4. For the second part, observe that Theorem A.3 provides an explicit method for constructing a winning strategy on _H_ given a strategy for a prior graph _G<sub>i</sub>_ such that \(G_i\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\).

## Generalized Büchi games.

A generalized Büchi game is equipped with a family of sets \(F_1,\dots,F_r\subseteq V\) , and Player 1 wins if every set _F<sub>i</sub>_ is visited infinitely often. Generalized Büchi games can be viewed as a special case of value-determined games. Indeed, if the sets _F_<sub>1</sub>_,...,F<sub>r</sub>_ come with fixed identifiers, we may label every vertex _v_ by the set

\(w(v):=\{i\in[r]|v\in F_i\},\)

and choose the Borel objective that requires every index \(i\in[r]\) to occur infinitely often. Hence, Theorem A.2 immediately applies to this representation.

There is, however, a subtlety in this formulation. Encoding the indices \(i\in[r]\) as part of the vertex labels makes the identities of the Büchi sets part of the input attributes. Consequently, an isomorphism is required to preserve every set _F<sub>i</sub>_ individually. This is stronger than the arguably more natural notion of isomorphism for generalized Büchi games, under which the Büchi sets themselves may be permuted. Namely, one would only require the existence of a graph isomorphism \(\varphi\) and a permutation \(\pi\) of \[_r_\] such that

\(v\in F_i\Longleftrightarrow\varphi(v)\in F'_{\pi(i)}\)

for every \(v\in V\) and \(i\in[r]\).

A natural attempt to model this stronger symmetry is to introduce one unlabeled auxiliary vertex for each Büchi set and encode membership by incidence edges. In such a representation, graph isomorphisms may freely permute the auxiliary vertices, exactly as desired. However, our current 1-WL argument does not immediately extend to this representation: the shadow-play construction preserves local colors and transition behavior, but does not provide a single globally consistent matching between the Büchi sets of the two games. Such a consistent matching appears necessary in order to conclude that visiting every Büchi set infinitely often is preserved.

### Rabin games.

A similar distinction arises for Rabin games. A Rabin game is equipped with a family of pairs (_E_<sub>1</sub>_,F_<sub>1</sub>)_,...,(E<sub>r</sub>,F<sub>r</sub>_), where \(E_i,F_i\subseteq V\) , and Player 1 wins if there exists an index \(i\in[r]\) such that _E<sub>i</sub>_ is visited only finitely often and _F<sub>i</sub>_ is visited infinitely often. If the pairs come with fixed identifiers, we may label every vertex _v_ by

\(w(v):=\big(\{i\in[r]|v\in E_i\},\{i\in[r]|v\in F_i\}\big).\)

The Rabin condition is then a Borel objective on the resulting label sequence, so Theorem A.2 also applies to this representation.

As in the generalized Büchi case, however, this encoding requires isomorphisms to preserve every set _E<sub>i</sub>_ and _F<sub>i</sub>_ individually. Under the more natural notion of isomorphism, the Rabin pairs may be permuted, while the pairing and the roles of their two components are preserved. More precisely, one requires a game-graph isomorphism \(\varphi\) and a permutation \(\pi\) of \[_r_\] such that

\(\varphi(E_i)=E'_{\pi(i)}\text{and}\varphi(F_i)=F'_{\pi(i)}\)

for every \(i\in[r]\). Encoding the pairs and their two types of membership using auxiliary vertices and incidence edges allows this symmetry to be represented. However, the same obstacle remains: our current shadow-play construction does not provide a single globally consistent correspondence between the Rabin pairs, and therefore does not establish preservation of the Rabin objective in this representation.

### Open questions.

Under the natural notions of isomorphism described above, we leave open whether the Isomorphic-Priors model admits algorithms with _O_(poly(_k,n_)) preprocessing time and

1. _O(n_<sup>2.99</sup>) query time for generalized Büchi games, when the Büchi sets may be arbitrarily permuted; and<tbc>

2. _O_(poly(_n_)) query time for Rabin games, when the Rabin pairs may be arbitrarily permuted.

## A.3 The Replacement Path Problem

The work of Vassilevska Williams and Williams \[VW10\] is widely regarded as an early landmark in fine-grained complexity. In particular, they showed that a number of fundamental problems with best known subcubic algorithms are tightly related via subcubic reductions, yielding an equivalence web among path, matrix, and triangle problems.

In this appendix, we show that, in our model, Replacement Path can be solved in _O_((_n+m_)log_n_) time.

**Definition A.4** (Replacement Path)**.** An instance of Replacement Path is defined by a tuple _G_=(_V,E,c,P_), where

• (_V,E_) is a finite directed graph,<tbc>

• \(c:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R}\) is a cost function assigning a non-negative cost to each edge,<tbc>

• _P=v_<sub>1</sub>_v_<sub>2</sub>_...v<sub>k</sub>_ is a shortest path.

The solution for Replacement Path is a vector _OPT_=(_OPT_<sub>1</sub>_,...,OPT_<sub>_k_-1</sub>), where for each \(i\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}\), _OPT<sub>i</sub>_ denotes the cost of the shortest _v_<sub>1</sub>_,v<sub>k</sub>_-path in _G<sub>i</sub>_=(_V,E_\\{(_v<sub>i</sub>,v_<sub>_i_+1</sub>)}).

_Remark_ A.5. We may assume without loss of generality that _G_ contains no negative cycles reachable from _v_<sub>1</sub> and to _v<sub>k</sub>_. Indeed, since _P_ is a shortest path, the distance between its endpoints is finite.

We view an instance _G_=(_V,E,c,P_), where _P=v_<sub>1</sub>_v_<sub>2</sub>_...v<sub>k</sub>_, of Replacement Path as an attributed graph with edge attributes \(\alpha_E(e)=c(e)\) for all \(e\in E\) and vertex attributes \(\alpha_V(v_i)=i\) for all \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\), and \(\alpha_V(w)=0\) for all other vertices \(w\in V\backslash\{v_1,\dots,v_k\}\).

**Theorem A.6** (Replacement Path in the Isomorphic-Priors Model)**.** _There is an algorithm that solves_ Replacement Path _with k prior instances each having at most n vertices and m edges in O(k(n+m_)log_n_) _preprocessing time and O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time. Additionally, if each prior G<sub>i</sub> is equipped with a set of replacement paths, then the algorithm can also compute a set of replacement paths for H in O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _time._

In the following theorem, we prove that Replacement Path is invariant under 1-WL equivalence.

**Theorem A.7.** _Let_ \(G=(V,E,c:E\rightarrow\mathbb{R},P)\) _and_ \(G'=(V',E',c':E'\rightarrow\mathbb{R},P')\) _be two instances of_ Replacement Path_. If_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G'\)_, then G and_ \(G'\) _have the same optimal replacement path vector._

_Proof._ Let _P=v_<sub>1</sub>_,...,v<sub>k</sub>_ and \(P'=v'_1,\dots,v'_k\) be the designated shortest paths in _G_ and \(G'\), respectively. Observe that the initial coloring \(\chi_0\) assigns color _i_ to _v<sub>i</sub>_ and to \(v'_i\) for every \(i\in\{1,\dots,k\}\), and assigns color 0 to all remaining vertices. Let _OPT_ and \(OPT'\) be the optimal replacement vectors for _G_ and \(G'\), respectively. We show that for every \(i\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}\), \(OPT_i=OPT'_i\).

Fix \(i\in\{1,\dots,k-1\}\). Let _Q=u_<sub>1</sub>_,...,u<sub>m</sub>_ be a shortest _v_<sub>1</sub>_,v<sub>k</sub>_-path in _G<sub>i</sub>_=(_V,E_\\{(_v<sub>i</sub>,v_<sub>_i_+1</sub>)}). We construct a \(v'_1,v'_k\)-walk \(Q'=u'_1,\dots,u'_m\) in \(G'_i=(V',E'\backslash\{(v'_i,v'_{i+1})\})\) with the same sequence of stable colors as _Q_, and hence with the same total cost.

We define \(Q'\) inductively. Since _u_<sub>1</sub>=_v_<sub>1</sub>, its initial color is 1. Because \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}G'\), there exists a vertex \(u'_1\in V'\) with \(\chi_\infty^G(u_1)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(u'_1)\). By the Refinement property of 1-WL (see Lemma 7.6), \(u'_1\) has the same initial color as _u_<sub>1</sub>, and therefore \(\chi_0^{G^\prime}(u'_1)=1\), so \(u'_1=v'_1\).

Now suppose that \(u'_j\) has already been chosen so that \(\chi_\infty^G(u_j)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(u'_j)\). Since \((u_j,u_{j+1})\in E\), by Neighborhood Preservation (see Lemma 7.6), there exists an outgoing edge \((u'_j,u'_{j+1})\in E'\) such that \(\chi_\infty^G(u_{j+1})=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(u'_{j+1})\) and (_u<sub>j</sub>,u_<sub>_j_+1</sub>) and \((u'_j,u'_{j+1})\) have the same edge label, i.e., the same cost under _c_ and \(c'\), respectively. Continuing in this way, we obtain a walk \(Q'\) in \(G'\) from \(v'_1\) to some vertex \(u'_m\) with \(\chi_\infty^G(v_k)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(u'_m)\). By Refinement, \(\chi_0^{G^\prime}(u'_m)=\chi_0^G(v_k)=k\), and hence \(u'_m=v'_k\).

Thus, \(Q'\) is a \(v'_1,v'_k\)-walk in \(G'\) and \(c'(Q')=c(Q)\). We claim that \(Q'\) does not use the edge \((v'_i,v'_{i+1})\). Suppose otherwise. Then there exists _j_ such that \((u'_j,u'_{j+1})=(v'_i,v'_{i+1})\). Since \(v'_i\) and \(v'_{i+1}\) are the unique vertices of initial colors \(\chi_0^{G^\prime}(v'_i)=i\) and \(\chi_0^{G^\prime}(v'_{i+1})=i+1\), it follows from \(\chi_\infty^G(u_j)=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(u'_j)\) and \(\chi_\infty^G(u_{j+1})=\chi_\infty^{G^\prime}(u'_{j+1})\), together with another application of Refinement, that _u<sub>j</sub>=v<sub>i</sub>_ and _u_<sub>_j_+1</sub>=_v_<sub>_i_+1</sub>. Hence (_u<sub>j</sub>,u_<sub>_j_+1</sub>)=(_v<sub>i</sub>,v_<sub>_i_+1</sub>), contradicting the fact that _Q_ is a path in _G<sub>i</sub>_.

Therefore, \(Q'\) is a valid \(v'_1,v'_k\)-walk in \(G'_i\), and so, by Remark A.5, \(OPT'_i\le c'(Q')=c(Q)=OPT_i\). By symmetry, \(OPT_i\le OPT'_i\). Hence \(OPT_i=OPT'_i\), as required.

_Proof of Theorem A.6._ The first part follows directly from Theorems A.7 and 8.4. For the second part, observe that Theorem A.7 provides an explicit method for constructing replacement paths on _H_ given replacement paths for a prior graph _G<sub>i</sub>_ such that \(G_i\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\).

## A.4 Maximum Flow

Next, we show that Maximum Flow can be solved in near-linear time in our model, slightly improving over existing worst-case algorithms \[CKL<sup>+</sup>22, vdBCP<sup>+</sup>23, vdBLL<sup>+</sup>21, vdBLN<sup>+</sup>20\]. Towards this end, we again argue that 1-WL equivalent graphs admit the same maximum flow. We note that this also improves over a result from \[AM13\] where the same is shown for 2-WL.

**Definition A.8.** An instance of Maximum Flow is a tuple _G_=(_V,E,c,s,t_) where (_V,E_) is a directed graph, \(c:E(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) are edge capacities, and \(s,t\in V\) are the source and sink vertex. A _flow_ is a mapping \(f:E(G)\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\) such that

• \(f(e)\le c(e)\) for all \(e\in E(G)\), and<tbc>

• \(\sum_{u\in N_{in}(v)}f(u,v)=\sum_{w\in N_{out}(v)}f(v,w)\) for all \(v\in V\backslash\{s,t\}\).

The objective is to find a flow _f_ that maximizes \(\mathrm{val}(f):=\sum_{w\in N_{out}(s)}f(s,w)\).

**Theorem A.9** (Maximum Flow in the Isomorphic-Priors Model)**.** _There is an algorithm that solves_ Maximum Flow _with k prior instances each having at most n vertices and m edges in O(k(n+m_)log_n_) _preprocessing time and O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time. Additionally, if each prior G<sub>i</sub> is equipped with a maximum flow, then the maximum flow for the query graph can be found in O_((_n+m_)log_n_) _query time._

For the proof, we require some additional basic tools. First, we generalize the neighborhood preservation property from Lemma 7.6.

**Lemma A.10** (Folklore)**.** _For every two (attributed) graphs_ \(G=(V_G,E_G,\alpha_G^V,\alpha_G^E)\) _and_ \(H=(V_H,E_H,\alpha_H^V,\alpha_H^E)\) _such that_ \(G\equiv_{1\text{-WL}}H\)_, the following holds:_

1. **_Neighborhood Multiset Preservation:_** _For every_ \(v\in V_G\) _and_ \(v'\in V_H\)_, if_ \(\chi_\infty^G(v)=\chi_\infty^H(v')\)_, then for every stable color C and edge attribute_ \(\ell\)_, it holds that_<tbc>

<tbc>\(\left|\left\{u\in V_G|\alpha_G^E(u,v)=\ell,\chi_\infty^G(u)=C\right\}\right|=\left|\left\{u'\in V_H|\alpha_H^E(u',v')=\ell,\chi_\infty^H(u')=C\right\}\right|.\)<tbc>

<tbc>_The analogous statement holds for outgoing edges._

Now let _G_=(_V,E,c,s,t_) be an instance of Maximum Flow, and let \(\chi_\infty^G\) denote the coloring computed by 1-WL. We define an auxiliary instance \(G/\chi_\infty=(V^*,E^*,c^*,s^*,t^*)\) via

• \(V^*=\{\chi_\infty^G(v)|v\in V\}\),<tbc>

• \(E^*=\{(\chi_\infty^G(v),\chi_\infty^G(w))|(v,w)\in E\}\),<tbc>

• \(c^*(a,b)=\sum_{v\in\chi^{-1}(a),w\in\chi^{-1}(b),(v,w)\in E}c(v,w)\),<tbc>

• \(s^*=\chi_\infty^G(s)\) and \(t^*=\chi_\infty^G(t)\).

The next two lemmas prove that the value of the maximum flow is identical in _G_ and \(G/\chi_\infty\).

**Lemma A.11.** _Let G_=(_V,E,c,s,t_) _be an instance of_ Maximum Flow _and let f be a flow in G. Then there exists a flow f_<sup>∗</sup> _in_ \(G/\chi_\infty\) _such that_ \(\mathrm{val}(f^*)\ge\mathrm{val}(f)\).

_Proof._ For \((a,b)\in E(G/\chi_\infty)\), we define

## B More Conditional Lower Bounds

### B.1 Additional Problem Definitions

**Definition B.1** (0/1-Integer Linear Programming)**.** In the 0/1-Integer Linear Programming we are given an integer matrix _C_ and an integer _d_ and. We have to decide if there exist a 0/1-vector _x_ with _Cx=d_.

Two problem instances (_C,d_) and \((C',d')\) are isomorphic if there are permutation matrices _P_ and _Q_ with \(PCQ=C'\) and \(Pd=d'\).

Note that 0/1-Integer Linear Programming is closed under isomorphism since if _x_ is a solution to _Cx=d_ if and only if \(x'=Q^{-1}x\) is a solution to \(C'x'=d'\). For the remaining problem checking that they are closed under isomorphism is easy to see.

**Definition B.2** (_k_-Center)**.** In the _k_-Center problem we are given a simple graph _G_=(_V,E,w_) with edge weights \(w:E\rightarrow\mathbb{N}\), a number \(k\in\mathbb{N}\), and a value \(c\in\mathbb{N}\). We have to decide if there is a set \(X\subseteq V\) of size at most _k_ such that every \(v\in V\) has distance at most _c_ to the closest point in _X_.

Two problem instances (_G_=(_V,E,w),k,c_) and \((G'=(V',E',w'),k',c')\) are isomorphic if \(k=k'\), \(c=c'\) and _G_ is isomorphic to \(G'\).

**Definition B.3** (Clique)**.** In the Clique problem we are given a simple graph _G_ and a value _k_. We have to decide if _G_ contains _k_-clique (i.e., a subgraph with _k_ vertices such that each vertex is connected to each other vertex)

Two problem instances (_G,k_) and \((G',k')\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs and \(k=k'\).

**Definition B.4** (Clique Cover)**.** In the Clique Cover problem we are given a simple graph _G_ and a value _k_. We have to decide if _G_ contains clique cover of size at most _k_ (i.e., there is a collection of at most _k_ many cliques that are all subgraphs of _G_ and each edge of _G_ is covered by at least one clique)

Two problem instances (_G,k_) and \((G',k')\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs and \(k=k'\).

**Definition B.5** (Coloring)**.** In the Coloring problem we are given a simple graph _G_ and a value _k_. We have to decide if _G_ is _k_-colorable.

Two problem instances (_G,k_) and \((G',k')\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs and \(k=k'\).

**Definition B.6** (_k_-Coloring)**.** In the _k_-Coloring problem we are given a simple graph _G_. We have to decide if _G_ is _k_-colorable.

Two problem instances _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs.

**Definition B.7** (3D-Matching)**.** In the 3D-Matching problem we are given a set \(U\subseteq[n]^3\). We have to decide if there exist a set \(W\subseteq U\) with |_W_|=_n_ and no two elements of _W_ agree in any coordinate.

Two problem instances (_U,n_) and \((U',n')\) are isomorphic if there exist a bijection \(f:[n]\rightarrow[n']\) with \(U'=\{(f(x),f(y),f(z))|(x,y,z)\in[n]^3\}\).

**Definition B.8** (Exact Cover)**.** In the Exact Cover problem we are given a number _n_ and a values of subsets \(S_1,\dots,S_m\subseteq[n]\). We have to decide if there are indices _j_<sub>1</sub>_,...j<sub>s</sub>_ such that _S_<sub>_j_<sub>1</sub></sub>_,...,S<sub>j<sub>s</sub></sub>_ are disjoint and \(\bigcup_{t=1}^sS_{j_t}=\bigcup_{i=1}^mS_i\).

Two problem instances (_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>m</sub>,n_) and \((S'_1,\dots,S'_{m^\prime},n')\) are isomorphic if \(m=m'\), \(n=n'\) and there are bijective functions \(f:[n]\rightarrow[n']\) and \(g:[m]\rightarrow[m']\) such that for each \(i\in[m]\) we obtain \(f(S_i)=\{f(s)|s\in S_i\}=S'_{g(j)}\)

**Definition B.9** (Feedback Arc Set)**.** In the Feedback Arc Set problem we are given a directed graph _H_ and a number _k_. We have to decide if there exist a set of edges \(S\subseteq E(G)\) with \(|S|\le k\) such that every cycle in _G_ contains at least on edge in _S_.

Two problem instances (_H,k_) and \((H',k')\) are isomorphic if \(k=k'\) and \(H\cong H'\) are isomorphic as graphs.

**Definition B.10** (Feedback Vertex Set)**.** In the Feedback Vertex Set problem we are given a directed graph _H_ and a number _k_. We have to decide if there exist a set of vertices \(R\subseteq V(G)\) with \(|R|\le k\) such that every cycle in _G_ contains at least on vertex in _R_.

Two problem instances (_H,k_) and \((H',k')\) are isomorphic if \(k=k'\) and \(H\cong H'\) are isomorphic as graphs.

**Definition B.11** (Directed Hamiltonian Cycle)**.** In the Directed Hamiltonian Cycle problem we are given a directed unweighted graph _G_. We have to decide if _G_ contains a directed cycle which includes each node exactly once.

Two problem instances _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs.

**Definition B.12** (Undirected Hamiltonian Cycle)**.** In the Undirected Hamiltonian Cycle problem we are given a undirected unweighted graph _G_. We have to decide if _G_ contains a directed cycle which includes each node exactly once.

Two problem instances _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs.

**Definition B.13** (Hitting Set)**.** In the Hitting Set problem we are given a number _n_ and a values of subsets \(S_1,\dots,S_k\subseteq[n]\). We have to decide if there is a set \(W\subseteq[n]\) such that \(|W\cap S_i|=1\).

Two problem instances (_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>k</sub>,n_) and \((S'_1,\dots,S'_{k^\prime},n')\) are isomorphic if \(k=k'\), \(n=n'\) and there are bijective functions \(f:[n]\rightarrow[n']\) and \(g:[k]\rightarrow[k']\) such that for each \(i\in[k]\) we obtain \(f(S_i)=\{f(s)|s\in S_i\}=S'_{g(j)}\)

**Definition B.14** (Independent Set (IS))**.** In the Clique problem we are given a simple graph _G_ and a value _k_. We have to decide if _G_ contains an independent set of size _k_ (i.e., a subgraph with _k_ vertices such that no vertex is connected to any other vertex)

Two problem instances (_G,k_) and \((G',k')\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs and \(k=k'\).

**Definition B.15** (MaxCut)**.** In the MaxCut problem we are given a simple graph _G_ and a value _k_. We have to decide if there exist a subset of vertices \(S\subseteq V(G)\) such that there are at least _k_ many edges between _S_ and _V(G_)\\_S_.

Two problem instances (_G,k_) and \((G',k')\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs and \(k=k'\).

**Definition B.16** (_k_-Median)**.** In the _k_-Median problem we are given a set of facilities _F_={_f_<sub>1</sub>_,...,f<sub>t</sub>_}, a set of clients _C_={_c_<sub>1</sub>_,...,c<sub>s</sub>_}, a function \(d:F\times C\rightarrow\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}\), that satisfies the triangle inequality, a number _k_ and a number _c_. We have to decide if there are exist a set \(F'\subseteq F\) of size _k_ such that

\(\sum_{i=1}^smin_{f\in F^\prime} d(f,c_i)\le c.\)

Two problem instances (_F,C,d,k,c_) and \((F',C',d',k',c')\) are isomorphic if \(c=c'\), \(k=k'\), and there are bijections \(f:F\rightarrow F'\) and \(g:C\rightarrow C'\) such that \(d(x,y)=d'(f(x),g(y))\).

**Definition B.17** (Satisfiability (SAT))**.** In the Satisfiability problem we are given a formula \(\Phi\) in conjunctive normal form (CNF). We have to decide if \(\Phi\) is decidable.

Two CNF formulas \(\Phi\), \(\Phi'\) are isomorphic if \(\Phi'\) can be obtained from \(\Phi\) by a renaming of variables. Note that this renaming is consistent with negation (i.e., if we rename _x_ to _y_ then \(\neg x\) is mapped to \(\neg y\)).

**Definition B.18** (3-Satisfiability (3-SAT))**.** In the 3-Satisfiability problem we are given a formula \(\Phi\) in conjunctive normal form (CNF) such that each clause contains exactly three literals. We have to decide if \(\Phi\) is decidable.

Two CNF formulas \(\Phi\), \(\Phi'\) are isomorphic if \(\Phi'\) can be obtained from \(\Phi\) by a renaming of variables. Note that this renaming is consistent with negation (i.e., if we rename _x_ to _y_ then \(\neg x\) is mapped to \(\neg y\)).

**Definition B.19** (Max _k_-SAT)**.** In the Max _k_-SAT we are given a formula \(\Phi\) in conjunctive normal form (CNF) such that each clause contains exactly _k_ literals. Given an assignment _x_ of variables we write \(|\Phi(x)|\) for the number of clauses that are satisfied by _x_. We have to return \(max_x|\Phi(x)|\).

Two CNF formulas \(\Phi\), \(\Phi'\) are isomorphic if \(\Phi'\) can be obtained from \(\Phi\) by a renaming of variables. Note that this renaming is consistent with negation (i.e., if we rename _x_ to _y_ then \(\neg x\) is mapped to \(\neg y\)).

**Definition B.20** (Set Cover)**.** In the Set Cover problem we are given a number _n_, a list of subsets \(S_1,\dots,S_m\subseteq[n]\), and a number _k_. We have to decide if there are indices _j_<sub>1</sub>_,...j<sub>s</sub>_ such that \(s\le k\) and \(\bigcup_{t=1}^sS_{j_t}=\bigcup_{i=1}^mS_i\).

Two problem instances (_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>m</sub>,n,k_) and \((S'_1,\dots,S'_{m^\prime},n',k')\) are isomorphic if \(m=m'\), \(k=k'\), \(n=n'\) and there are bijective functions \(f:[n]\rightarrow[n']\) and \(g:[k]\rightarrow[k']\) such that for each \(i\in[m]\) we obtain \(f(S_i)=\{f(s)|s\in S_i\}=S'_{g(i)}\).

**Definition B.21** (Set Packing)**.** In the Set Packing problem we are given a family of sets S={_S_<sub>1</sub>_,...,S<sub>m</sub>_} with \(S_i\subseteq[n]\) and a number _k_. We have to decide if there exist _k_ many mutually disjoint sets in S.

Two problem instances (S=(_S_1_,...,Sm),n,k_) and (S=(_S_1_,...,Sm),n,k_) are isomorphic if \(m=m'\), \(k=k'\), \(n=n'\) and there are bijective functions \(f:[n]\rightarrow[n']\) and \(g:[k]\rightarrow[k']\) such that for each \(i\in[m]\) we obtain \(f(S_i)=\{f(s)|s\in S_i\}=S'_{g(i)}\). **Definition B.22** (Steiner Tree)**.** In the Steiner Tree problem we are given a weighted undirected graph _G_, set of vertices _R_, and a value _k_. We have to decide if _G_ contains a subtree that contains each vertex in _R_ and has cost (i.e. sum of edges) at most _k_. Two problem instances (_G,R,k_) and \((G',R',k')\) are isomorphic if \(k=k'\) and there is an isomorphism \(\varphi:V(G)\rightarrow V(G')\) from _G_ to \(G'\) that respects the edge weights and \(\varphi\) maps _R_ to \(R'\). **Definition B.23** (Traveling Salesman Problem (TSP))**.** In the Traveling Salesman Problem we are given a weighted clique with _n_ vertices where each edge-weight is non-negative. We have to return the length of the humiliation cycle with the smallest length. Two problem instances _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic if the underlying graphs are isomorphic. **Definition B.24** (Metric Traveling Salesman Problem (Metric TSP))**.**
In the Metric Traveling Salesman Problem we are given a weighted clique with _n_ vertices where each edge-weight is non-negative. Further the edge-weight satisfy the triangle inequality. We have to return the length of the humiliation cycle with the smallest length. Two problem instances _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic if the underlying graphs are isomorphic. **Definition B.25** (Vertex-Cover (VC))**.** In the Vertex-Cover problem we are given a simple graph _G_ and a value _k_. We have to decide if _G_ contains a vertex cover of size at most _k_. Two problem instances (_G,k_) and \((G',k')\) are isomorphic if _G_ and \(G'\) are isomorphic as graphs and \(k=k'\). ## B.2 Additional Isomorphism-Preserving Reductions In the following we show many different isomorphism-preserving reductions.
